title: He Was Struck Silent
subtitle: Luke 1:1–25
description: Luke opens like an investigator, then takes us into the temple, where an old priest hears the first good news in four hundred years and comes out unable to speak.
paragraphs: Luke is the only Gospel writer who shows you his method before he shows you his story. “Many have undertaken to compose an account of the things that have been fulfilled among us,” he writes, accounts handed down by “the initial eyewitnesses and servants of the word.” His own work stands on theirs and on his research: “having carefully investigated everything from the beginning,” he decided “to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus,” and he states his purpose in one sentence: “so that you may know the certainty of the things you have been taught.” Only after the method comes the story, and the story opens not in Rome or even in Jerusalem's streets, but in the temple, with an old priest whose name means the Lord remembers.

“In the time of Herod king of Judea there was a priest named Zechariah, who belonged to the priestly division of Abijah, and whose wife Elizabeth was a descendant of Aaron.” Luke's verdict on the couple is complete and kind: “Both of them were righteous in the sight of God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and decrees of the Lord.” Then he sets down the sorrow the whole chapter will answer, in the same flat tone: “But they had no children, because Elizabeth was barren, and they were both well along in years.” Righteous, blameless, and childless in a culture that read barrenness as disgrace. They have carried it for decades, and they have kept serving anyway.

The day that changes everything is an ordinary duty day raised by lot to the honor of a lifetime. Zechariah's division is on duty, and “he was chosen by lot, according to the custom of the priesthood, to enter the temple of the Lord and burn incense.” Inside the sanctuary he offers the incense at the golden altar; outside, “the whole congregation was praying outside,” the hour of incense being an hour of prayer for everyone. An old priest might wait his whole career for this lot to fall to him, and many never got it. Then, at the right side of the altar of incense, an angel of the Lord is standing there, and Zechariah is startled and gripped with fear.

The angel's first word is about prayer, an old prayer, the one underneath all the years: “Do not be afraid, Zechariah, because your prayer has been heard. Your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you are to give him the name John.” The promise grows past the nursery as Gabriel speaks. “He will be a joy and delight to you, and many will rejoice at his birth,” and the boy will live under a Nazirite-like rule: “He shall never take wine or strong drink,” and “he will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb.” The mission is national, not merely domestic: he will turn many of Israel back to their God, going before the Lord “in the spirit and power of Elijah,” “to turn the hearts of the fathers to their children” and to make ready a prepared people. Four hundred years of prophetic silence, and the first word from heaven is the last word of the old book come true: a son, named John, going before the Lord.

Zechariah believes the angel is real. What he cannot yet believe is the arithmetic. “How can I be sure of this?” Zechariah asked the angel. “I am an old man, and my wife is well along in years.” The answer names the speaker and hands down the sign at once: “I am Gabriel,” replied the angel. “I stand in the presence of God, and I have been sent to speak to you and to bring you this good news.” The sign is silence: “And now you will be silent and unable to speak until the day this comes to pass,” because he did not believe words that would be fulfilled at their proper time. Outside, the congregation is wondering at the delay, and when Zechariah finally emerges he can only make signs to them, and “they realized he had seen a vision in the temple.” He finishes his days of service and goes home, still silent. In the house in the hill country, Elizabeth conceives and keeps herself in seclusion five months, and her one recorded word in this episode is gratitude with the disgrace lifted: “The Lord has done this for me. In these days He has shown me favor and taken away my disgrace among the people.” The Lord remembers. It was his name all along.

title: Favored One
subtitle: Luke 1:26–56
description: Gabriel visits a young woman in Nazareth, the Spirit overshadows her, and two mothers meet in the hill country with a song on the younger one's lips.
paragraphs: Six months into Elizabeth's hidden pregnancy, heaven speaks again, this time in a town nobody would have chosen. “In the sixth month, God sent the angel Gabriel to a town in Galilee called Nazareth, to a virgin pledged in marriage to a man named Joseph, who was of the house of David. And the virgin’s name was Mary.” Gabriel's greeting is the episode's title and its puzzle: “Greetings, you who are highly favored! The Lord is with you.” Mary is not comforted by it. She is greatly troubled, and wonders what kind of greeting this might be. Before she has said a word, the angel answers the trouble, not the silence: “Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God.”

The announcement outruns anything a favored girl in Nazareth could have framed. “Behold, you will conceive and give birth to a son, and you are to give Him the name Jesus.” Then the titles pile up, each one larger than the last: “He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. The Lord God will give Him the throne of His father David, and He will reign over the house of Jacob forever. His kingdom will never end!” David's throne, Jacob's house, a kingdom without end, promised to a child not yet conceived, in a village that appears in no earlier Scripture. Mary's response is a question, and it matters that hers differs from Zechariah's. He asked how he could be sure. She asks how it can happen at all: “How can this be,” Mary asked the angel, “since I am a virgin?”

Gabriel answers the how with the Holy Spirit and offers the sign she did not request. “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. So the Holy One to be born will be called the Son of God.” And the sign is her cousin: Elizabeth, called barren all her life, “is in her sixth month,” carrying a son in her old age. The ground under the promise is one line: “For no word from God will ever fail.” Mary's answer is the hinge of the chapter, and Luke gives it without commentary: “I am the Lord’s servant,” Mary answered. “May it happen to me according to your word.” Then the angel left her, and the favored one gets up and travels.

She hurries to the hill country of Judah, to Zechariah's house, and the meeting of the two mothers becomes a meeting of the two children. At the sound of Mary's greeting, the baby in Elizabeth leaps, and Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, cries out the confirmation Mary has told no one: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb!” She names her own place in the story with wonder: “And why am I so honored, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” The mother of my Lord, spoken by the older woman over the younger, before any public word has been said anywhere. Elizabeth's last line blesses the belief itself: “Blessed is she who has believed that the Lord’s word to her will be fulfilled.”

Then Mary sings, and her song is a revolution sung in the past tense, as if God has already done it all. “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior! For He has looked with favor on the humble state of His servant. From now on all generations will call me blessed. For the Mighty One has done great things for me. Holy is His name.” The mercy runs generation to generation; the arm of God scatters the proud, pulls rulers from their thrones, and lifts the humble. “He has filled the hungry with good things, but has sent the rich away empty.” It is Hannah's song grown up, Israel's whole hope compressed into a young woman's voice in a hill country house, ending where it began, with the promise “to Abraham and his descendants forever.” Mary stays about three months, long enough to see Elizabeth nearly to her term, and then returns home to Nazareth, to face everything the favor will cost.

title: His Name Is John
subtitle: Luke 1:57–80
description: A baby is named by a written word, a silenced father's mouth opens, and his song runs from his own house to the sunrise from on high.
paragraphs: Elizabeth's time comes, and the disgrace of decades ends in a son. The neighbors and relatives hear that the Lord has shown her great mercy, and they rejoice with her, the same community that once read her barrenness as a verdict now reading her child as mercy. On the eighth day they gather to circumcise the boy, and everyone present assumes the naming is a formality: he will be Zechariah, after his father. The mother who has waited longest speaks first, and she is not tentative. “No! He shall be called John.” The relatives push back on the facts: there is no one among the family who bears that name. So they turn, with signs, to the father, the silent man at the edge of his own son's naming, to ask what he wants to call the child.

Zechariah asks for a writing tablet, and what he writes is not a suggestion. “His name is John.” Not shall be, but is: the name was settled in the temple, by the God who sent Gabriel, and the father's nine months of silence end in agreement with it. “Immediately Zechariah’s mouth was opened and his tongue was released, and he began to speak, praising God.” The first use of the returned voice is praise, and the effect runs outward through the whole hill country: awe on the neighbors, talk in every village, and one question repeated wherever the story travels: “What then will this child become?” Luke answers it himself in a single line: “For the Lord’s hand was with him.”

Then the old priest, filled with the Holy Spirit, prophesies, and his song, the Benedictus, looks in two directions. First it looks backward and up: “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, because He has visited and redeemed His people. He has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of His servant David,” spoken through the prophets, promised in the oath to Abraham, mercy to the fathers across every generation. The goal of it all is worship without fear: deliverance, Zechariah sings, so that God's people may serve Him “in holiness and righteousness before Him all the days of our lives.” The song is about the coming King before it is about the baby in the room.

Only then does the father turn to his own son, and the boy's job description is given as plainly as Gabriel gave it: “And you, child, will be called a prophet of the Most High; for you will go on before the Lord to prepare the way for Him, to give to His people the knowledge of salvation through the forgiveness of their sins.” Not the forgiveness itself, but the knowledge of it, the announcement ahead of the arrival. The song ends in the dark turning toward morning: because of the tender mercy of God, “the Dawn will visit us from on high, to shine on those who live in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the path of peace.”

Luke closes the chapter where he will leave the boy for thirty years. “And the child grew and became strong in spirit; and he lived in the wilderness until the time of his public appearance to Israel.” No more visits, no more songs on record. The forerunner grows up in the desert his message will come out of, and the story Luke is telling swings away from the hill country house to an empire and a decree, and a town called Bethlehem.

title: Good News of Great Joy
subtitle: Luke 2:1–20
description: An emperor's decree moves a family to Bethlehem, and the announcement of the birth goes first to shepherds on the night watch.
paragraphs: Luke frames the birth of Jesus inside the machinery of an empire. “Now in those days a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that a census should be taken of the whole empire.” He dates it in his own way, the first census “while Quirinius was governor of Syria,” and the decree sets the whole world walking to be registered. Among the walkers is a carpenter from Nazareth: “So Joseph also went up from Nazareth in Galilee to Judea, to the city of David called Bethlehem, since he was from the house and line of David.” With him is Mary, pledged to him, expecting a child. An emperor counts his world for taxes, and the counting carries David's heir to David's town, where Micah said the ruler would come from. Neither Caesar nor Joseph is thinking about Micah.

While they are there, the days are completed, and Luke tells the birth itself with a restraint that has become famous. “And she gave birth to her firstborn, a Son. She wrapped Him in swaddling cloths and laid Him in a manger, because there was no room for them in the inn.” No midwife, no scene painted, just a mother wrapping her baby in strips of cloth the way village mothers did, and a feeding trough for a cradle because the guest room was full. The King whose kingdom will never end is announced to no court, laid where animals eat, in the town of David, unnoticed by everyone in it.

The announcement, when it comes, goes to shepherds on the night shift outside the town, men at the bottom of the social order, keeping watch over their flocks. An angel stands before them, the glory of the Lord shines around them, and they are terrified. But the angel said to them, “Do not be afraid! For behold, I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people: Today in the city of David a Savior has been born to you. He is Christ the Lord!” Savior, Christ, Lord, the three titles stacked into one sentence over a field. And the sign given to verify it is not a wonder but a baby in the same ordinary wrappings: “You will find a baby wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger.”

Then the sky fills. “And suddenly there appeared with the angel a great multitude of the heavenly host, praising God and saying: ‘Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men on whom His favor rests!’” When the angels return into heaven, the shepherds do the only sensible thing: “Let us go to Bethlehem and see this thing that has happened, which the Lord has made known to us.” They hurry off and find it exactly so, Mary and Joseph and the baby lying in the manger. And having seen, they become the first preachers of the Gospel in Luke: they spread the message they had received about the child, and everyone who hears it is amazed.

One person in the story does something other than speak. “But Mary treasured up all these things and pondered them in her heart.” The angel's titles, the shepherds' report, the heavenly host: she stores them, turning them over, the first theologian of her own son. The shepherds go back to their fields changed: “The shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen, which was just as the angel had told them.” The sign held. The word was verified in a stable, by night workers, before it was ever heard in a synagogue.

title: A Light for Revelation
subtitle: Luke 2:21–52
description: Simeon and Anna recognize the child in the temple, and twelve years later his parents find him there again, among the teachers.
paragraphs: Luke keeps the child inside the law of Moses at every step. On the eighth day he is circumcised and named Jesus, “the name the angel had given Him before He was conceived.” When the days of purification are complete, his parents bring him up to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord, under the written rule: “Every firstborn male shall be consecrated to the Lord.” The sacrifice they offer tells its own quiet story: “A pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons,” the offering the law allowed to families who could not afford a lamb. The Son of the Most High is consecrated in the temple by poor parents, with the poor family's birds in hand.

In the temple courts that day is a man who has been waiting for this appointment his whole life. Simeon is righteous and devout, “waiting for the consolation of Israel,” and he carries a private promise: the Holy Spirit had revealed to him that “he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ.” Led by the Spirit into the courts at the right hour, he takes the child in his arms and blesses God with a song of dismissal: “Sovereign Lord, as You have promised, You now dismiss Your servant in peace. For my eyes have seen Your salvation, which You have prepared in the sight of all people, a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to Your people Israel.” A light for the Gentiles, said over a Jewish baby in the temple, in the hearing of his astonished parents. The watchman has seen what he waited for and is ready to die.

But Simeon has a second word, and it is for the mother, and it is not all comfort. “Behold, this Child is appointed to cause the rise and fall of many in Israel, and to be a sign that will be spoken against,” he tells Mary, the child a dividing line through his own nation, “so that the thoughts of many hearts will be revealed.” And then to her personally, the first shadow across the story: “and a sword will pierce your soul as well.” Simeon blesses them and steps back into the silence of the text, his promise kept. He is not the only elder waiting in the temple. Anna, a prophetess, widowed for decades after seven years of marriage, now eighty-four, “never left the temple, but worshiped night and day, fasting and praying.” Coming forward at that very moment, she gives thanks to God and speaks about the child “to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem.”

The family returns to Nazareth, and Luke covers eighteen years in a sentence: the child grows strong, filled with wisdom, “the grace of God was upon Him.” One scene survives from those years, at Passover, when he is twelve. The caravan goes home without him; a day out, his parents discover he is not among the relatives, and three days of searching end in the temple, where they find him “sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions,” with everyone who hears him astounded at his understanding and his answers. His mother does the talking, as anxious parents do: “Child, why have You done this to us?” His mother asked. “Your father and I have been anxiously searching for You.” His reply is the first recorded sentence of Jesus in any Gospel: “Why were you looking for Me?” He asked. “Did you not know that I had to be in My Father’s house?”

They do not understand the statement, Luke says plainly, and the boy goes down to Nazareth with them anyway and is obedient to them, and his mother does again what she did at his birth: she treasures all these things in her heart. The episode and the childhood close on Luke's summary, balanced like a scale: “And Jesus grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and man.” Ahead of him are a baptism, a genealogy, and a voice from a wilderness. Behind him, two old saints in a temple have already said the largest things that will ever be said about him.

title: Prepare the Way for the Lord
subtitle: Luke 3:1–20
description: John preaches repentance at the Jordan, answers the crowds' question with specifics, and points past himself to the stronger One.
paragraphs: Luke dates the word of God like a historian and then sends it to a desert. “In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar,” with Pontius Pilate governing Judea, Herod tetrarch of Galilee, his brother Philip and Lysanias ruling their territories, “during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas, the word of God came to John son of Zechariah in the wilderness.” Seven rulers are named between heaven and John, every seat of power in the world Luke's readers knew, and the word goes to none of them. It goes to the silenced priest's son in the desert, who “went into all the region around the Jordan, preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins,” exactly where Isaiah had put the voice: “Prepare the way for the Lord, make straight paths for Him.” Luke quotes Isaiah all the way to the promise his whole book will keep: “And all humanity will see God’s salvation.”

John's preaching to the crowds who come out is not gentle. “You brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?” The baptism he offers is not a charm against judgment; it demands evidence. “Produce fruit, then, in keeping with repentance.” And he cuts the ground from under the oldest excuse in Israel: do not start saying “We have Abraham as our father,” because “out of these stones God can raise up children for Abraham.” Descent is not fruit. The warning ends with an axe: “The axe lies ready at the root of the trees, and every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.”

What makes Luke's account of John distinct is what happens next: the crowds take him seriously, and his answers are concrete, economic, and near at hand. “What then should we do?” “Whoever has two tunics should share with him who has none, and whoever has food should do the same.” Tax collectors come, of all people, and ask the same question, and he does not tell them to quit the tax booth; he tells them, “Collect no more than you are authorized.” Soldiers ask, and the answer is, “Do not take money by force or false accusation,” and, “Be content with your wages.” Repentance, in John's preaching, looks like honesty at the toll booth, restraint with a sword, and an open hand at the wardrobe. No one is sent to a mountain. Everyone is sent home different.

The crowds begin to wonder whether John himself might be the Christ, and he answers the speculation by pointing past himself, as he was born to do. “I baptize you with water, but One more powerful than I will come, the straps of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire.” Luke keeps the fire in John's promise, and the fire has a picture with it: “His winnowing fork is in His hand to clear His threshing floor and to gather the wheat into His barn; but He will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.” Wheat gathered, chaff burned: the coming One will separate as well as save. With many other exhortations, Luke says, John proclaimed the good news to the people.

One man in the crowds' world does not repent, and John does not exempt him. He rebukes Herod the tetrarch “regarding his brother’s wife Herodias and all the evils he had done,” the marriage and everything behind it, and Herod's answer is to add one more evil to the list: “He locked John up in prison.” Luke sets the forerunner's arrest down here, at the head of the story, before Jesus has done anything in public at all. The voice is silenced into a cell, the way prepared, and the one John pointed to steps forward to be baptized among the people he came to save.

title: The Son of Adam, the Son of God
subtitle: Luke 3:21–38
description: Heaven opens over the praying Jesus, and Luke traces his line upward past Abraham and David all the way to Adam, and to God.
paragraphs: Luke tells the baptism almost in passing, and adds the detail only he records: it happened while Jesus was praying. “When all the people were being baptized, Jesus was baptized too. And as He was praying, heaven was opened, and the Holy Spirit descended on Him in a bodily form like a dove. And a voice came from heaven: ‘You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased.’” He is baptized with the people, not apart from them, one more figure in the Jordan crowds who came confessing sins he did not have. Heaven answers the prayer with the same declaration Matthew recorded, spoken to Jesus himself. The ministry that is about to begin opens with the Father's voice, and then, immediately, with a list of names.

“Jesus Himself was about thirty years old when He began His ministry.” Before Luke narrates a single sermon or miracle, he inserts the genealogy, and he runs it backward and far beyond where Matthew stopped. “He was regarded as the son of Joseph, the son of Heli, the son of Matthat, the son of Levi,” name behind name, generation behind generation, climbing the centuries. The word “regarded” carries the whole of Luke's honesty in the roll: this is Joseph's line, the legal line, and Joseph is the father the world supposed. Luke states it the way the record stands and lets the annunciation, told two chapters earlier, say the rest.

The line passes David by a different son than Matthew used. Where Matthew's genealogy descended from David through Solomon the king, Luke's climbs up through “the son of Mattatha, the son of Nathan, the son of David,” Nathan, a son of David who never reigned. The two rolls agree on David and on Abraham; they differ in the names between, and Luke does not smooth the difference or explain it, and neither does this telling. Both stand in the series side by side, each as its writer wrote it. Up the names go through the judges' age and the exodus and the patriarchs: “the son of Jacob, the son of Isaac, the son of Abraham,” and still the roll does not stop, because Luke is not finished climbing.

Past Abraham the names reach men no Israelite roll needed: Noah of the flood, Enoch who walked with God, Seth. And then the last links, the ones no other genealogy in Scripture attempts: “the son of Enosh, the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God.” The roll that began with a carpenter in Nazareth ends at the creation itself. Adam is called a son of God, and Jesus is set down as Adam's heir, which is Luke's whole Gospel in one list: this Savior belongs not to one nation's family tree but to the human race's. The angel's phrase over the Bethlehem field, good news “for all the people,” turns out to have been a genealogy before it was a sermon.

It is characteristic of Luke that he puts this roll here, between the baptism and the temptation, and then does nothing with it at all. No sermon follows it, no explanation. The names stand, seventy-seven of them, and the story moves on into the wilderness, where the Son of Adam will be tested the way the first Adam was, in a place of hunger, with the same ancient voice asking its questions.

title: Forty Days in the Wilderness
subtitle: Luke 4:1–13
description: Full of the Spirit and led by the Spirit, Jesus faces three offers in the desert and answers each from Deuteronomy, ending at Jerusalem's height.
paragraphs: “Then Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit into the wilderness, where for forty days He was tempted by the devil.” Luke keeps the account short and orders it his own way, and the order matters: his temptation ends not on a mountain but at the temple. The fast comes first. “He ate nothing during those days, and when they had ended, He was hungry,” and into the hunger the devil speaks the same opening he used in Matthew: “If You are the Son of God, tell this stone to become bread.” The stones of the wilderness look like loaves; the Son of God is starving; the suggestion wears the clothes of common sense. Jesus answers out of Deuteronomy, the book of Israel's own wilderness: “It is written: ‘Man shall not live on bread alone.’”

The second temptation is instant and total. The devil leads him up and shows him “in an instant all the kingdoms of the world,” and names his price with a claim Jesus does not dispute in the exchange: “I will give You authority over all these kingdoms and all their glory,” he said. “For it has been relinquished to me, and I can give it to anyone I wish. So if You worship me, it will all be Yours.” The kingdoms Jesus came to win, offered without the cross: bow once, and skip the road to Jerusalem entirely. The answer is again Deuteronomy, and again worship is the whole issue: “It is written: ‘Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only.’”

For the last test Luke takes him where Matthew's account does not end: to Jerusalem, to the pinnacle of the temple, the city and the house where this Gospel began. “If You are the Son of God,” he said, “throw Yourself down from here.” And this time the devil quotes Scripture himself, Psalm 91, God's own promise of angelic guard: “For it is written: ‘He will command His angels concerning You to guard You carefully, and they will lift You up in their hands, so that You will not strike Your foot against a stone.’” The temptation has changed weapons: not appetite, not ambition, but the Word of God bent into a dare, a staged miracle at the temple to force the Father's hand and the city's faith at once. Jesus answers the quotation with a command: “It also says, ‘Do not put the Lord your God to the test.’” Scripture is not a lever to move God. It is the ground to stand on.

Luke's last line on the wilderness is the coldest of any Gospel: “When the devil had finished every temptation, he left Him until an opportune time.” Every temptation, finished; the devil, not destroyed but departed, waiting for a better opening. The opportune time will come in a garden and in a council chamber three years later. For now Jesus walks out of the desert the way he walked in, full of the Spirit, and Luke turns him toward Galilee and the synagogue of his own hometown, where the next test will be of a different kind: not the devil's voice, but the voices of the people who raised him.

title: The Kingdom Proclaimed
subtitle: Luke 4:14–5:11
description: A Nazareth sermon ends at a cliff edge, demons are silenced in Capernaum, and a failed night's fishing becomes the call of the first disciples.
paragraphs: Luke lifts Nazareth to the front of the ministry as a program statement. Jesus comes home, enters the synagogue on the Sabbath as was his custom, stands to read, and is handed the scroll of Isaiah. He unrolls it to a passage and reads: “The Spirit of the Lord is on Me, because He has anointed Me to preach good news to the poor. He has sent Me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to release the oppressed, to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor.” Then he stops, mid-passage, before Isaiah's day of vengeance, rolls the scroll back up, hands it to the attendant, and sits down with every eye in the room fixed on him. His sermon is one sentence: “Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing.”

The room warms to the gracious words, and then turns on the familiarity: “Isn’t this the son of Joseph?” Jesus answers the turn before it finishes, naming what they want: “Physician, heal yourself! Do here in Your hometown what we have heard that You did in Capernaum.” Miracles as a hometown dividend. His reply reaches for the two most uncomfortable stories in the prophets: in the famine, “Elijah was not sent to any of them, but to the widow of Zarephath in Sidon,” a foreigner; and in Elisha's time, of all the lepers in Israel, “not one of them was cleansed,” only Naaman the Syrian. Grace that skips the insiders for outsiders. The synagogue fills with rage, drives him out of town to the brow of the hill, and means to throw him off the cliff. “But Jesus passed through the crowd and went on His way,” and the ministry moves to Capernaum and does not come back.

In Capernaum the words have weight. The people are astonished “because His message had authority,” and the authority is tested at once by a man in the synagogue with an unclean spirit, who cries out what the hometown would not consider: “What do You want with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have You come to destroy us?” and then, naming him outright, “I know who You are,” he cries, “the Holy One of God!” Jesus silences him and commands him out; the demon throws the man down and leaves without harming him, and the question spreads with the news: “What is this message? With authority and power He commands the unclean spirits, and they come out!” The day ends at Simon's house, where the fever is rebuked out of Simon's mother-in-law and she rises and serves them, and at sunset the whole town's sick are carried to the door and healed one by one, each with his hands laid on them.

At daybreak he withdraws to pray, and when the crowds find him and try to keep him, he refuses to be kept: “I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well, because that is why I was sent.” Beside the Lake of Gennesaret the pressing crowd sends him into Simon's boat for a pulpit, and afterward he gives the professional an order that makes no professional sense: “Put out into deep water and let down your nets for a catch.” Simon states the facts and obeys anyway: “Master,” Simon replied, “we have worked hard all night without catching anything. But because You say so, I will let down the nets.” The catch tears nets, fills two boats to sinking, and Simon Peter falls at Jesus' knees with the opposite of a disciple's request: “Go away from me, Lord,” he said, “for I am a sinful man.” The answer turns the kneeling fisherman toward his life: “Do not be afraid,” Jesus said to Simon. “From now on you will catch men.” They beach the boats, leave the great catch and everything with it, and follow him.

title: New Wine into New Wineskins
subtitle: Luke 5:12–39
description: A leper is touched, a paralytic is lowered through a roof, a tax collector hosts a feast, and the new wine bursts the old arrangements.
paragraphs: The leper who opens this stretch does not demand; he submits the whole matter to Jesus' will and only states the ability as fact: “Lord, if You are willing, You can make me clean.” Jesus answers with touch before words, reaching out his hand to a man no one had touched in years: “I am willing,” He said, and commanded him to be clean, and immediately the leprosy left him. The cleansed man is sent to the priest with Moses' offering, as a testimony to them, and ordered to silence. The silence does not hold; it never does in Luke. The news spreads all the more, great crowds gather to hear and to be healed, and against the pressure Luke sets down one of his signature lines: “Yet He frequently withdrew to the wilderness to pray.” The fame and the prayer grow together, each apparently requiring the other.

The paralytic arrives through the roof because there is no other way in. The house is packed with Pharisees and teachers of the law from Jerusalem and every village of Galilee and Judea, and the friends on the roof lower their man on his mat through the tiles, into the middle of the crowd, right in front of Jesus. What Jesus says first is not about legs: “Friend, your sins are forgiven.” The scribes and Pharisees reason silently, and accurately, by their theology: “Who can forgive sins but God alone?” Jesus answers the thought out loud: “Which is easier: to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Get up and walk’?” Then, “so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on the earth to forgive sins,” he turns to the paralytic: “I tell you, get up, pick up your mat, and go home.” The man stands immediately before them all, takes up the mat, and goes home glorifying God, and the crowd's verdict has a note of wonder Luke loves: “We have seen remarkable things today.”

Then Jesus walks out and calls a tax collector, Levi at his booth, with two words, and Levi leaves everything and follows him, and throws a great banquet at his house with a large crowd of tax collectors at the table. The Pharisees complain to the disciples about the company, and Jesus answers for his own table: “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick. I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners, to repentance.” A doctor's defense: his place is among the sick. It is the theology of every banquet in this Gospel stated early, in one sentence, at a tax collector's table.

The fasting question follows, since John's disciples fast and his feast. The bridegroom saying answers it, as in the other Gospels: the guests cannot fast while the bridegroom is with them, but “the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast.” Then come the two pictures, patch and wineskins, and Luke adds the saying's hard tail. No one tears a patch from a new garment for an old one; “no one pours new wine into old wineskins,” for the skins will burst and both be lost; “new wine is poured into new wineskins.” And then the line only Luke records, aimed at every settled taste that hears him: “And no one after drinking old wine wants new, for he says, ‘The old is better.’” The kingdom's newness will not be refused only by enemies. It will be refused by people who simply prefer what they have already tasted.

title: Lord of the Sabbath
subtitle: Luke 6:1–19
description: Grain plucked on the Sabbath, a withered hand restored in full view, a night of prayer, and twelve apostles named at morning.
paragraphs: The Sabbath controversies arrive in Luke in a pair. Hungry disciples walk through grainfields on the Sabbath, picking heads of grain, rubbing them in their hands, and eating, and the Pharisees' charge is about work on the holy day: “Why are you doing what is unlawful on the Sabbath?” Jesus answers from the Scriptures they are defending, with David on the run eating the consecrated bread: “Have you not read what David did when he and his companions were hungry? He entered the house of God, took the consecrated bread and gave it to his companions, and ate what is lawful only for the priests to eat.” Then he ends the argument not with a ruling but with a rank: “The Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.” The question is not what the day permits. It is who the day belongs to.

On another Sabbath, in a synagogue, the watchers set their own trap. A man with a withered right hand is present, and the scribes and Pharisees watch Jesus closely “to see if He would heal on the Sabbath,” looking for a reason to accuse him. Jesus knows their thoughts and stages the whole thing in the open: the man is called up to stand among them all. The question is put to the room: “I ask you, which is lawful on the Sabbath: to do good or to do evil, to save life or to destroy it?” No one answers. After looking around at all of them, he says to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” The hand is restored whole, in front of the trap-setters, on the day in question. “But the scribes and Pharisees were filled with rage and began to discuss with one another what they might do to Jesus.” Doing good on the Sabbath has now become, in their accounting, the destroying kind of act.

What Jesus does next is the pattern Luke keeps showing: he withdraws from the rage into prayer, and the prayer is long. “In those days Jesus went out to the mountain to pray, and He spent the night in prayer to God.” Only when daylight comes does he call the disciples and choose twelve of them, “whom He also designated as apostles”: Simon renamed Peter, and Andrew; James and John; Philip and Bartholomew; Matthew and Thomas; James son of Alphaeus and Simon the Zealot; Judas son of James; and the list ends the way Luke's story will end, with “Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor” named from the start. A night of prayer does not screen out the betrayer. He is chosen with the rest, after the whole night, with open eyes.

Then Jesus comes down with the twelve and stands “on a level place,” and Luke paints the crowd before a word of the sermon: a large company of disciples, and a great number of people from all Judea and Jerusalem and the seacoast of Tyre and Sidon, Gentile country, who had come to hear him and to be healed of their diseases. “The entire crowd was trying to touch Him, because power was coming from Him and healing them all.” On level ground, with the sick pressing in and power going out of him, he looks up at his disciples and begins the sermon that defines his kingdom. It starts with a word no one expected to hear pronounced over poverty: Blessed.

title: Blessed Are You Who Are Poor
subtitle: Luke 6:20–49
description: On a level place the blessings come with matching woes, love of enemies is commanded, and the sermon ends with two foundations.
paragraphs: Luke's sermon is preached on a plain, to disciples, in the hearing of the crowds, and it opens with four blessings that reverse the world's ledger. “Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.” Not poor in spirit, as Matthew has it; poor, full stop, the people in front of him with nothing. “Blessed are you who hunger now, for you will be filled. Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh.” And for the hated and excluded: “Blessed are you when people hate you, and when they exclude you and insult you and reject your name as evil because of the Son of Man.” Then, uniquely in Luke, the blessings are answered by four woes aimed the other way: “But woe to you who are rich, for you have already received your comfort. Woe to you who are well fed now, for you will hunger. Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep.” The sermon is a great reversal announced in advance: now is not the final state of anyone in the crowd.

The ethics that follow are built for people living among enemies. “But to those of you who will listen, I say: Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, pray for those who mistreat you.” The struck cheek is turned, the taken cloak is followed by the tunic, the asker is given to and the taker is not chased for return. Underneath the examples sits the Golden Rule in its positive form: “Do to others as you would have them do to you.” And three times Jesus asks the deflating question of ordinary reciprocity: if you love those who love you, “what credit is that to you? Even sinners love those who love them.” Kingdom love is measured by what it does for those who can return nothing: “love your enemies, do good to them, and lend to them, expecting nothing in return.” The reason given is family resemblance: the Most High “is kind to the ungrateful and wicked.” Then the whole section lands in a single sentence: “Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful.”

Judging is treated as a boomerang. “Do not judge, and you will not be judged. Do not condemn, and you will not be condemned. Forgive, and you will be forgiven.” And giving is treated as a measure that comes back on the giver: “Give, and it will be given to you. A good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over will be poured into your lap. For with the measure you use, it will be measured back to you.” The picture is a market measure heaped past fairness, the generous standard applied to the generous.

The closing parables turn the hearer into the examined. A blind guide leads another blind man into a pit. And the eye surgery everyone attempts: “Why do you look at the speck in your brother’s eye but fail to notice the beam in your own eye?” The tree test follows: “each tree is known by its own fruit,” figs not gathered from thornbushes nor grapes from brambles, the good man bringing good out of the good treasure of his heart: “For out of the overflow of the heart the mouth speaks.” Then the sermon drives at the gap between address and obedience: “Why do you call Me ‘Lord, Lord,’ but do not do what I say?”

It ends with two builders. The one who hears and acts “dug down deep and laid his foundation on the rock,” and when the flood came and the torrent crashed against the house, it could not shake it. The one who hears and does not act built on bare ground, and when the torrent struck, the house fell immediately, “and great was its destruction.” Luke's sermon does not close with a blessing but with a collapse. The words have been spoken on level ground to level hearers, and the only question the sermon leaves open is the one it was built to ask: not whether you heard, but what you dug.

title: Young Man, I Say to You, Arise
subtitle: Luke 7:1–17
description: A centurion's faith amazes Jesus without a meeting, and a widow's only son sits up in his coffin at a word.
paragraphs: Luke's centurion never comes to Jesus himself; his faith travels by messengers from first to last, and it is all the stronger for it. His servant, highly valued, is sick and about to die, and the centurion sends Jewish elders to plead for him. The elders argue his worthiness like advocates: “This man is worthy to have You grant this, for he loves our nation and has built our synagogue.” A Roman officer who built a synagogue for the people he occupies: he has spent money and love on Israel's God, and now he spends his hope on Israel's teacher. Jesus goes with them at once, without a word of discussion. The worthiness case has been made by friends, and Jesus does not cross-examine it.

Near the house a second delegation arrives with the opposite argument, and this one is the centurion's own faith speaking. “Lord, do not trouble Yourself, for I am not worthy to have You come under my roof. That is why I did not consider myself worthy to come to You. But just say the word, and my servant will be healed.” The elders pleaded that he was worthy; the man insists he is not, and his unworthiness is built on a soldier's logic about authority: “For I myself am a man under authority, with soldiers under me. I tell one to go, and he goes, and another to come, and he comes. I tell my servant to do something, and he does it.” A word from an authorized man travels and accomplishes; Jesus' word, he reasons, needs no journey at all. Jesus marvels, the only time in Luke he is said to do so, and turns to the Jewish crowd following him with the verdict: “I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such great faith.” The messengers return to the house and find the servant well. Distance was nothing. The word had done it before they arrived.

Then Luke takes Jesus to Nain, and a funeral procession walks out of the town gate as the procession of life walks in. The dead man is “the only son of his mother, and she was a widow”: every word of that description is a loss. Her husband is gone, now her only son, and with him her future and her keep. A large crowd from the town is with her, and it cannot do anything but walk. “When the Lord saw her, He had compassion on her,” and he speaks first not to the corpse but to the mother, telling her not to weep, a sentence no one at a funeral has the right to say unless he can back it. Then he steps up and touches the coffin, and the bearers stand still. “Young man,” He said, “I tell you, get up!” The dead man sits up and begins to speak, and Luke's sentence of restoration is domestic and total: “Then Jesus gave him back to his mother.” Elijah returned a widow's son in Zarephath; at Nain it happens again, without the asking.

Awe sweeps the crowd, and their interpretation runs to the prophets and to the old visitation language of Scripture: “A great prophet has appeared among us!” they said. “God has visited His people!” The news spreads through Judea and the surrounding region. Note what the two halves of this episode share: a Gentile officer's servant healed without touch, without presence, almost without a word spoken on the scene, and a widow's son raised with touch and a word and nothing asked. Faith is honored at a distance in the first; compassion acts unasked in the second. Luke's Jesus answers both the man who believes hard and the woman who, so far as the record says, believes nothing yet at all.

title: Her Many Sins Have Been Forgiven
subtitle: Luke 7:18–50
description: John sends a question from prison, Jesus defends the Baptist and weeps over a generation, and a sinful woman washes his feet with her tears.
paragraphs: John the Baptist, locked in Herod's prison, hears reports that do not match the axe he preached, and he sends two disciples with the question his whole ministry hangs on: “Are You the One who was to come, or should we look for someone else?” Jesus does not answer yes or no. At that very hour he is healing diseases and afflictions and evil spirits and giving sight to the blind, and his answer is a list of evidence drawn from Isaiah: “Go back and report to John what you have seen and heard: The blind receive sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the good news is preached to the poor.” The widow's son at Nain is inside that list, freshly raised. Then comes the tender warning to the imprisoned prophet: “Blessed is the one who does not fall away on account of Me.” The works are the answer; the offense is the risk.

To the crowds Jesus then gives John's eulogy, and it is unsparing in both directions. “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed swaying in the wind?” Not a reed, and not a palace courtier: a prophet, “and more than a prophet,” the messenger of Malachi who prepares the way. The verdict on John's rank is the highest Jesus gives any man: “among those born of women there is no one greater than John, yet even the least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.” The tax collectors in the crowd, baptized by John, acknowledge God's justice; the Pharisees and experts in the law, unbaptized, have rejected God's purpose for themselves. On that rejection Jesus hangs the picture of the generation: children in the marketplace who will neither dance to the flute nor weep to the dirge. “We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not weep.” John came fasting and they called him demon-possessed; the Son of Man came eating and drinking and they call him a glutton and a friend of sinners. “But wisdom is vindicated by all her children.”

The episode ends at a Pharisee's table, where the friend-of-sinners charge is enacted. Simon has invited Jesus to dinner, and a woman of the town, a sinner by reputation, learns where he is dining and comes in uninvited with an alabaster jar of perfume. She stands behind him at his feet, weeping, and her tears wet his feet, and she wipes them with her hair, and kisses them, and pours the perfume over them. Simon watches and draws the reasonable conclusion in his heart: “If this man were a prophet, He would know who this is and what kind of woman is touching Him,” for she is a sinner. Jesus answers the unspoken thought with a name: “Simon, I have something to tell you.”

The parable is a moneylender's ledger: two debtors, one owing five hundred denarii, one fifty, neither able to pay, both forgiven. “Which one, then, will love him more?” Simon's answer is careful and slightly reluctant: “I suppose the one who was forgiven more.” “You have judged correctly,” Jesus said, and then turns toward the woman and reads Simon his own omissions off her devotion: no water for the feet, but her tears; no kiss of greeting, but her unceasing kisses; no oil for the head, but her perfume on the feet. The conclusion overturns the table's whole judgment: “Therefore I tell you, her many sins have been forgiven, for she has loved much. But he who has been forgiven little loves little.” To the woman herself he speaks the word the host was sure he would not: “Your sins are forgiven.” The other guests murmur the episode's recurring question, who is this who even forgives sins, and Jesus dismisses the woman with the last word of the scene: “Your faith has saved you; go in peace.”

title: The Seed on Good Soil
subtitle: Luke 8:1–21
description: The women who fund the ministry are named, the sower's seed falls on four soils, and Jesus redraws the boundaries of family.
paragraphs: Before the parable, Luke names the people bankrolling the ministry, and the list is one of his signatures. Jesus travels from town to village preaching the kingdom, the Twelve with him, “as well as some women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out, Joanna the wife of Herod’s household manager Chuza, Susanna, and many others.” The wife of Herod's steward travels with the movement her household serves the enemy of, and Luke's summary is financial: “These women were ministering to them out of their own means.” Healed women fund the preaching. The kingdom runs on their money, a fact the other Gospels leave in footnotes and Luke puts in the text.

To the crowds gathering town after town he tells the sower, in his own version. The seed on the path is trampled and eaten by birds; the seed on rock springs up and withers for lack of moisture; the seed among thorns is choked as it grows; the seed on good soil produces a crop, a hundredfold. “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.” Asked for the meaning, Jesus first gives the reason for parables themselves, the Isaiah sentence about seeing without seeing, and then decodes his own story, beginning with its key: “The seed is the word of God.” The path people hear, and the devil takes the word from their hearts before it can save them. The rocky hearers “receive it with joy, but they have no root. They believe for a season, but in the time of testing, they fall away.” The thorny hearers are “choked by the worries, riches, and pleasures of this life, and their fruit does not mature.” Luke's three failures are theft, shallowness, and slow suffocation, and his good soil is defined by character and by time: “those with a noble and good heart, who hear the word, cling to it, and by persevering produce a crop.” Persevering is Luke's word. The crop comes to those who hold on.

The lamp saying belongs to the same teaching: what is lit is not hidden, and hidden things are coming into the light anyway. “No one lights a lamp and covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed. Instead, he sets it on a stand, so those who enter can see the light.” Then the warning about listening itself, which is the sower's point from the hearer's side: “Pay attention, therefore, to how you listen. Whoever has will be given more, but whoever does not have, even what he thinks he has will be taken away from him.” Hearing is not a neutral act in this Gospel; it enlarges or it shrinks the hearer.

The short scene that closes the chapter applies the parable to family. His mother and brothers arrive and cannot reach him through the crowd, and the message is passed in: “Your mother and brothers are standing outside, wanting to see You.” The reply redraws the family line around the word just preached: “My mother and brothers are those who hear the word of God and carry it out.” It is the sower as a household: kinship to Jesus is not by standing outside as relatives, but by hearing and doing, the good soil of the parable walking on two feet. Mary, who treasured and pondered, hears her own description spoken to a crowd.

title: Do Not Be Afraid; Only Believe
subtitle: Luke 8:22–56
description: A storm is stilled, a legion is drowned, a bleeding woman is named daughter, and a twelve-year-old is told to get up.
paragraphs: The lake crossing turns dangerous the way the Sea of Galilee can turn: a windstorm comes down, the boat swamps, and Jesus is asleep through it. The disciples wake him with the formal address of men who still are not sure who is in the boat: “Master, Master, we are perishing!” He gets up and rebukes the wind and the raging waters, and they subside, and all is calm. His question to the men in the sudden quiet is about them, not the weather: “Where is your faith?” Frightened and amazed, they ask the question Mark's crew also asked, the question the Gospel keeps asking: “Who is this? He commands even the winds and the water, and they obey Him!”

On the far shore, in the Gerasenes, a naked man who lives among the tombs meets him, possessed and unbindable, chains broken, driven by the demon into solitary places. He falls before Jesus shouting: “What do You want with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg You not to torture me!” The demons inside him beg not to be ordered into the Abyss, a detail Luke keeps, and beg instead for the herd of pigs on the hillside. Permission given, the herd rushes down the bank and drowns. The herdsmen run the news into town, and the townspeople come out and find the man who had been Legion “sitting at Jesus’ feet, clothed and in his right mind; and they were afraid.” The fear wins: all the people of the region ask Jesus to leave them. The delivered man begs to go with him and is instead commissioned on the spot: “Return home and describe how much God has done for you.” The first evangelist to the Decapolis is sent home, not along, and he proclaims through the town how much Jesus had done for him.

Back across the lake, a synagogue leader named Jairus is waiting, and falls at Jesus' feet begging for his only daughter, twelve years old, who is dying. On the way, the crowd presses so tightly that a touch registers: a woman with twelve years of bleeding, who had spent all her money on physicians without anyone able to heal her, comes up behind him and touches the fringe of his cloak, and her bleeding stops immediately. “Who touched Me?” Jesus asked. Everyone denies it, and Peter states the obvious: “Master,” said Peter, “the people are crowding and pressing against You.” But Jesus is certain: “Someone touched Me, for I know that power has gone out from Me.” The woman, seeing she cannot escape notice, comes trembling and tells the whole truth in front of everyone, why she touched him and how she was healed. His word to her is the episode's comfort spoken twice in the chapter: “Daughter,” said Jesus, “your faith has healed you. Go in peace.”

The delay has done its work, humanly speaking: a messenger arrives with the news no father survives hearing, and the advice that sounds like kindness, do not bother the Teacher anymore. Jesus overhears, and answers the death before he answers the death's report: “Do not be afraid; just believe, and she will be healed.” In the house he takes only Peter, John, and James and the parents in, past the mourners already weeping and wailing, and disputes their diagnosis: she is not dead, he says, but asleep. They laugh at him, knowing she is dead. He takes the child by the hand and calls out, “Child, get up!” Her spirit returns, she rises at once, and his last recorded instruction in the scene is beautifully ordinary: she is to be given something to eat. Her parents are astounded, and under orders to tell no one what has happened. A dead girl eats dinner; a healed woman walks home in peace; a delivered man preaches in his own town; and Luke stacks the three side by side without comment, the lake on one side and the lake on the other.

title: Five Loaves and Two Fish
subtitle: Luke 9:1–17
description: The Twelve are sent out with nothing, Herod is perplexed, and five loaves feed five thousand men beside Bethsaida.
paragraphs: Luke's sending of the Twelve is spare. Jesus gives them “power and authority over all demons, and power to cure diseases,” and sends them to proclaim the kingdom and heal, with an equipment list of nothing: “Take nothing for the journey,” He told them, “no staff, no bag, no bread, no money, no second tunic.” Houses will feed them; towns that refuse them will get the dust shaken off as testimony. They go village to village doing it, and the reports reach Herod, who is perplexed by the resurrection rumors around Jesus until his own guilt resolves the identity question his way: “I beheaded John,” Herod said, “but who is this man I hear such things about?” And he kept trying to see Jesus, a curiosity Luke leaves hanging over the story until a courtroom in Jerusalem finally grants it.

The apostles return and report, and Jesus takes them away privately toward Bethsaida to rest, but the crowds find out and follow, and Luke's sentence about the welcome matters: “He welcomed them and spoke to them about the kingdom of God, and He healed those who needed healing.” The withdrawal becomes a workday. As evening comes the Twelve bring their logistics: dismiss the crowd to find lodging and food: “For we are in a desolate place here.” Jesus hands the problem back to its presenters: “You give them something to eat.” The inventory is stated plainly: “We have only five loaves of bread and two fish,” unless the apostles are to go buy food for everyone. About five thousand men are present. He has the crowd seated in groups of about fifty, an arrangement that will make the distribution and the counting possible.

Then the familiar movements, done deliberately in sight of everyone: taking the five loaves and the two fish, looking up to heaven, speaking a blessing, breaking them, and giving them to the disciples to set before the people, again and again, the breaking never outrunning the supply. “They all ate and were satisfied, and the disciples picked up twelve basketfuls of broken pieces that were left over.” Luke tells one feeding of a multitude in his Gospel, this one, and tells it whole: five loaves, two fish, five thousand men, everyone satisfied, twelve baskets over. The men who had been sent out with no bread have just distributed bread that did not run out, to a crowd in a desolate place, and the lesson of the sending and the lesson of the feeding are the same lesson, taught twice in one chapter: the kingdom's supply is not calculated from the carriers' pockets.

The chapter now pivots from the crowd to the confession. Off alone in prayer, with the disciples near, Jesus will ask who the crowds say he is, and then ask the question the whole Gospel has been building toward: what about you? The five thousand have been fed. The twelve are about to be told what the feeding will cost the Feeder.

title: Who Do You Say I Am?
subtitle: Luke 9:18–62
description: Peter confesses the Christ of God, glory breaks out on the mountain, and the road south demands everything from those who would follow.
paragraphs: The question is asked in prayer, as so much in Luke happens. “Who do the crowds say I am?” The disciples report the street answers: John the Baptist, Elijah, a prophet of old arisen, the same rumors that perplexed Herod. “But what about you?” Jesus asked. “Who do you say I am?” Peter answered, “The Christ of God.” Luke's form of the confession is the shortest of the Gospels, and it is met not with blessing but with a strict warning to tell no one, and with the first prediction, stated as necessity: “The Son of Man must suffer many things,” He said. “He must be rejected by the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and He must be killed and on the third day be raised to life.” The Christ of God, confessed at last, immediately defines his Christhood as suffering, rejection, death, and resurrection, in that order.

Then the invitation is opened to everyone, with its price written in: “If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow Me.” Daily is Luke's addition to the saying, the cross not a single dramatic moment but a repeating act. “For whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for My sake will save it. What does it profit a man to gain the whole world, yet lose or forfeit his very self?” The accounting of the feeding chapter comes due: five loaves fed thousands, but a man is not a crowd, and his soul is not fed by gaining the world that fed on loaves.

About eight days later, praying again on a mountain, with Peter, John, and James, his face changes appearance and his clothes become radiantly white, and Moses and Elijah appear in glory talking with him. Luke alone says what they talked about: “His departure, which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.” Departure, in the Greek, is exodus: Moses, who led the first exodus, discusses the second with the man who will accomplish it by dying. Peter, waking, proposes three shelters, Luke noting that he did not know what he was saying, and the cloud interrupts him as it did at Nazareth's cliff edge: “This is My Son, whom I have chosen. Listen to Him!” Then only Jesus is present, and the three keep the vision to themselves.

Down the mountain, a father cries out of the crowd: “Teacher, I beg You to look at my son, for he is my only child.” The disciples have failed with the boy's demon. Jesus' exclamation is the harshest sentence in the episode: “O unbelieving and perverse generation!” Jesus replied. “How long must I remain with you and put up with you? Bring your son here.” Even as the boy approaches, the demon convulses him; Jesus rebukes the spirit, heals the boy, and gives him back to his father, as at Nain. Into the marveling, Jesus plants the second prediction like a nail: “Let these words sink into your ears: The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men.” They do not understand; it is veiled from them; and they are afraid to ask. Instead they argue about which of them is the greatest, and he sets a child beside him: whoever welcomes this little child in his name welcomes him, and “whoever is the least among all of you, he is the greatest.” John reports an outside exorcist being stopped, and is corrected: “Do not stop him,” Jesus replied, “for whoever is not against you is for you.”

Then the book turns on its hinge. “As the day of His ascension approached, Jesus resolutely set out for Jerusalem.” Luke will take ten chapters to arrive. A Samaritan village refuses him lodging because his face is set toward Jerusalem, and James and John ask to call down fire from heaven on it; he rebukes them, and they go to another village. The rejection does not slow the road; it defines it. Along that road three volunteers are tested: to the eager one, “Foxes have dens and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has no place to lay His head”; to the one who would first bury his father, “Let the dead bury their own dead. You, however, go and proclaim the kingdom of God”; to the one who would first say farewell at home, “No one who puts his hand to the plow and then looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.” The journey to Jerusalem has begun, and it will not look back either.

title: He Appointed Seventy-Two Others
subtitle: Luke 10:1–24
description: Seventy-two are sent two by two, woes fall on the lake towns, and the returning messengers learn where joy really lives.
paragraphs: The mission widens. After the Twelve, “the Lord appointed seventy-two others and sent them two by two ahead of Him to every town and place He was about to visit,” advance teams for the journey he has just begun. The commissioning repeats the Twelve's pattern with its own sentences. “The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few. Ask the Lord of the harvest, therefore, to send out workers into His harvest.” They go as “lambs among wolves,” carrying no purse or bag or sandals, greeting no one on the road, bringing a word of peace to each house and staying where the peace rests. Their message in a welcoming town is twofold: heal the sick there, and tell them, “The kingdom of God is near you.” In a town that refuses them, the same nearness is announced from the street as testimony, dust wiped off, kingdom near anyway. Nearness in Luke is not conditional on the welcome it gets.

On the refusing towns Jesus pronounces the woes, and they are Galilean towns, his own mission field: “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the miracles that were performed in you had been performed in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes.” Even Sodom will fare better on that day than a town that hosted the kingdom and shrugged. Capernaum, his base, gets the fall of Babylon's taunt turned on it: lifted up to heaven? “No, you will be brought down to Hades!” The stakes are set by the chain of hearing: “Whoever listens to you listens to Me; whoever rejects you rejects Me; and whoever rejects Me rejects the One who sent Me.” To refuse the seventy-two is to refuse the sender of the Sender.

The teams return with joy, and their report is about power: “Lord, even the demons submit to us in Your name.” His answer confirms the victory and then corrects the joy: “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven.” Authority over snakes and scorpions and all the power of the enemy is real, given, and not the point. “Nevertheless, do not rejoice that the spirits submit to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” The register of heaven, not the scoreboard of the mission, is the ground of rejoicing. It is Luke's version of the lesson Peter learned at the lakeside: the catch is not the treasure; being known is.

Then Luke shows Jesus himself rejoicing, the only place the Gospels use this strong word of him, and it is in the Holy Spirit and it is a prayer: “I praise You, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because You have hidden these things from the wise and learned, and revealed them to little children. Yes, Father, for this was well-pleasing in Your sight.” The seventy-two nobodies have carried revelation the wise missed, and the Father's pleasure in hiding and revealing explains it. All things have been entrusted to the Son; the Father is known only through him. Turning privately to the disciples he blesses their senses: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see. For I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see but did not see it, and to hear what you hear but did not hear it.” Prophets and kings waited centuries for what fishermen and tax collectors are watching on a road south, with Jerusalem ahead and the cross at the end of it.

title: Who Is My Neighbor?
subtitle: Luke 10:25–42
description: A lawyer's test becomes the parable of the Samaritan, and a busy hostess learns the one thing necessary at Jesus' feet.
paragraphs: An expert in the law stands up to test Jesus, and asks the largest question a lawyer can ask: “Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?” Jesus returns the question to the man's own profession: what is written in the Law, how do you read it? The expert answers perfectly, joining Deuteronomy and Leviticus the way Jesus himself joins them elsewhere: “‘Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind’ and ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’” “You have answered correctly,” Jesus said. “Do this and you will live.” The answer is complete and the conversation should be over, but the expert needs a boundary for the second command, a definition that limits the liability. “But wanting to justify himself, he asked Jesus, ‘And who is my neighbor?’”

Jesus answers with a road. A man going down from Jerusalem to Jericho falls into the hands of robbers, who strip him, beat him, and leave him half dead on the most dangerous descent in Judea. “Now by chance a priest was going down the same road, but when he saw him, he passed by on the other side.” A Levite comes to the spot, sees him, and passes by on the other side. Two religious professionals, two acts of seeing, two crossings to the far side of the road. “But a Samaritan on a journey came upon him, and when he saw him, he had compassion.” The third seeing produces the opposite of the first two. The Samaritan, the hereditary enemy, does everything: he goes to the man, bandages the wounds with oil and wine, lifts him onto his own animal, walks him to an inn, cares for him through the night, and in the morning leaves two denarii with the innkeeper and an open account: “Take care of him,” he said, “and on my return I will repay you for any additional expense.”

Then Jesus reverses the lawyer's question entirely. He does not ask who counts as a neighbor to be loved; he asks, “Which of these three do you think was a neighbor to the man who fell into the hands of robbers?” The expert cannot even say the word Samaritan. “The one who showed him mercy,” he replied. The definition he wanted as a fence has come back as a mirror: neighbor is not a category of person out there, it is a thing you either become or refuse to become on the road in front of you. “Go and do likewise,” Jesus told him, and the test ends with the tester sent out under orders.

Luke follows the parable of mercy with a quiet house in a village, where the other half of the lawyer's answer is weighed. Martha welcomes Jesus in and works; her sister Mary “sat at the Lord’s feet listening to His message,” taking the disciple's seat, at the feet, in a place women were not usually found. Martha, distracted by all the preparations, makes her appeal to fairness: “Lord, do You not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her to help me!” The answer is gentle and immovable: “Martha, Martha,” the Lord replied, “you are worried and upset about many things. But only one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, and it will not be taken away from her.” Service and listening are not enemies in this Gospel; the banquet tables ahead will prove that. But the portion chosen at his feet has a security the kitchen cannot give or take away, and the expert's two commands turn out to have two postures: mercy on the road, and attention in the house.

title: Teach Us to Pray
subtitle: Luke 11:1–36
description: Luke's own Lord's Prayer, a midnight knock, the finger of God, and a warning about the light within.
paragraphs: The request comes from watching. A disciple who has just seen Jesus finish praying asks for the thing John's disciples got from John: “Lord, teach us to pray, just as John taught his disciples.” The prayer Jesus gives in Luke is shorter than Matthew's, five petitions in his own form, and it stands in this Gospel exactly as he taught it here: “Father, hallowed be Your name. Your kingdom come. Give us each day our daily bread. And forgive us our sins, for we also forgive everyone who sins against us. And lead us not into temptation.” Father first, bread daily, forgiveness flowing in both directions, and deliverance from the test. Luke does not expand it. He surrounds it instead with a story about shameless persistence.

A man at midnight, a traveler arrived, an empty pantry, and a neighbor's door knocked on at the worst hour. “Friend, lend me three loaves of bread, because a friend of mine has come to me on a journey, and I have nothing to set before him.” The answer from inside is every sleeper's answer: “Do not bother me. My door is already shut, and my children and I are in bed. I cannot get up to give you anything.” Jesus' verdict on the knocking is the teaching: “even though he will not get up to provide for him because of his friendship, yet because of the man’s persistence, he will get up and give him as much as he needs.” Then the triple promise, verbs in the present tense, keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking: “Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened to you.” And the Father is measured not against the grudging neighbor but against human fathers, who do not hand a son a snake for a fish or a scorpion for an egg: “how much more will your Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him!” In Luke, the great gift prayer receives is the Spirit himself.

From prayer the chapter turns to the Beelzebul charge, returned now in a new town: a mute demon expelled, the man speaking, and the accusation that the exorcisms run on Satan's power. The logic is demolished first: “Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste, and a house divided against a house will fall.” Then the counter-evidence turns into the chapter's largest claim: “But if I drive out demons by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.” Finger of God is Luke's phrase, an Exodus phrase, the magicians of Egypt conceding a power beyond their arts. The strong man, fully armed, guards his house until someone stronger overpowers him and divides the plunder. Neutrality is excluded in one sentence: “He who is not with Me is against Me, and he who does not gather with Me scatters.” And the swept-house warning follows for the merely emptied life: the unclean spirit returns with seven worse than itself, and “the final plight of that man is worse than the first.” Deliverance without occupation is a vacancy sign.

A woman in the crowd blesses the mother, calling out the womb and the breasts that nursed him, and Jesus redirects the blessing to the hearers, in the words this Gospel keeps using for family: “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it.” The sign-seekers are refused everything but Jonah: Nineveh repented at a reluctant prophet, the Queen of the South crossed the world for Solomon's wisdom, “and now One greater than Jonah is here,” and greater than Solomon too. The chapter closes with the lamp again, turned inward this time: the eye as the body's lamp, the light within that can itself be darkness. “Be careful, then, that the light within you is not darkness.” Prayer taught, demons answered, signs refused, and the last warning is about the instrument of seeing itself, the day before a dinner invitation will test exactly that.

title: Woe to You
subtitle: Luke 11:37–12:21
description: A dinner turns into six woes, leaven is named hypocrisy, and a rich fool's full barns meet their owner's last night.
paragraphs: The dinner begins with a skipped washing, and the host's surprise is the sermon. A Pharisee has invited Jesus to dine; Jesus reclines without the ceremonial washing first, and the Pharisee marvels. The Lord answers the marveling, not the meal: “Now you Pharisees clean the outside of the cup and dish, but inside you are full of greed and wickedness. You fools! Did not the One who made the outside make the inside as well?” The remedy he prescribes turns their purity logic inside out: give as alms what is within, and behold, everything will be clean for you. Then the woes begin, three on the Pharisees, each attaching to a practice they were proudest of. “Woe to you Pharisees! For you pay tithes of mint, rue, and every herb, but you disregard justice and the love of God.” The tithing was meticulous down to garden herbs; the justice and love were the tithe left unpaid. The second woe is for loving “the chief seats in the synagogues and the greetings in the marketplaces,” honor as a hobby. The third is the quietest and the worst: “you are like unmarked graves, which men walk over without even noticing,” sources of defilement no one can see to avoid.

An expert in the law, feeling the splash, objects that these things insult his guild too, and receives three woes of his own. “For you weigh men down with heavy burdens, but you yourselves will not lift a finger to lighten their load.” The tombs they build for the prophets are read as consent to the fathers who killed them: “They killed the prophets, and you build their tombs.” And the last woe names the gatekeeping itself: “For you have taken away the key to knowledge. You yourselves have not entered, and you have hindered those who were entering.” Luke's comment on the dinner is the sound of a trap being set for the rest of the Gospel: from that hour the scribes and Pharisees oppose him bitterly and ply him with questions, “waiting to catch Him in something He might say.”

Outside, the crowd has grown to many thousands, trampling one another, and Jesus speaks first to his disciples with the metaphor of the day: “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy.” What the cup speech said of dishes, the leaven says of influence: small, invisible, spreading, and eventually disclosed, for nothing concealed will stay concealed and whispers in inner rooms will be proclaimed from housetops. He teaches them whom to fear instead, the One with authority beyond the body's death, and then the sparrows and the numbered hairs, and the confession before the angels of God.
