Into this teaching a voice from the crowd cuts with a family grievance: “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.” Jesus refuses the role: “Man, who appointed Me judge or executor between you?” And the refusal becomes the occasion for the warning and the parable: “Watch out! Guard yourselves against every form of greed, for one’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions.” The rich fool's ground produces abundantly, and his soliloquy is all first person: “What shall I do, since I have nowhere to store my crops?” Then the plan, self-approved: “I will tear down my barns and will build bigger ones, and there I will store up all my grain and my goods.” His retirement speech to his own soul, eat, drink, and be merry, is interrupted by the only voice in the parable besides his own: “But God said to him, ‘You fool! This very night your life will be required of you. Then who will own what you have accumulated?’” The barns stand full the same night, owned by a dead man. Luke gives the moral himself: “This is how it will be for anyone who stores up treasure for himself but is not rich toward God.”

title: You Must Be Ready
subtitle: Luke 12:22–59
description: Ravens and lilies argue against worry, the little flock is promised the kingdom, and watchful servants keep their lamps burning.
paragraphs: Worry is answered with birds and flowers. “Therefore I tell you, do not worry about your life, what you will eat, or about your body, what you will wear. For life is more than food, and the body more than clothes.” The ravens neither sow nor reap nor store, “yet God feeds them. How much more valuable you are than the birds!” Worry's futility is measured in its smallest possible unit: “Who of you by worrying can add a single hour to his life?” The lilies follow: “Consider how the lilies grow: They do not labor or spin. Yet I tell you, not even Solomon in all his glory was adorned like one of these.” If God so clothes grass that is thrown into the furnace tomorrow, the argument runs, the anxiety of his own children is a failure of arithmetic about their Father. The nations strive after food and drink; “your Father knows that you need them. But seek His kingdom, and these things will be added unto you.”

Then the tone softens into one of the tenderest sentences in the Gospel: “Do not be afraid, little flock, for your Father is pleased to give you the kingdom.” The flock is little; the gift is a kingdom; the Father's mood is pleasure. The economics follow from the gift: sell possessions, give to the poor, make purses that do not wear out, “an inexhaustible treasure in heaven, where no thief approaches and no moth destroys. For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”

From treasure the teaching turns to time, and the key word becomes ready. Servants dressed for service with lamps burning, waiting for a master returning from a wedding banquet, blessed if found watching in the second or third watch, and blessed in a way that reverses the household: “he will dress himself to serve and will have them recline at the table, and he himself will come and wait on them.” The homeowner who knew the thief's hour would not have been broken into; the Son of Man comes at an hour no one expects. “You also must be ready, because the Son of Man will come at an hour you do not expect.” Peter asks whether the parable is for the disciples or everyone, and the answer is the manager parable: the faithful and wise steward feeding the household at the proper time, the abusive steward beating the servants and getting drunk, the master arriving unannounced. Its principle is the chapter's scale of judgment: “From everyone who has been given much, much will be required; and from him who has been entrusted with much, even more will be demanded.”

The last movement is fire and friction. “I have come to ignite a fire on the earth, and how I wish it were already kindled! But I have a baptism to undergo, and how distressed I am until it is accomplished!” The baptism ahead is the cross, named as a flood he must go under, and it divides before it unites: “Do you think that I have come to bring peace to the earth? No, I tell you, but division,” households split three against two down the middle of the family table. Then to the crowds, weather-wise and time-blind: “You hypocrites! You know how to interpret the appearance of the earth and sky. Why don’t you know how to interpret the present time?” A cloud in the west means rain, a south wind means heat, and the signs are read correctly every day; the present time stands unread. The closing counsel is legal and urgent: settle with your adversary on the way to the magistrate, while there is still a road to settle on, for “you will not get out until you have paid the very last penny.” Readiness, in Luke, is not a mood. It is reconciliation done now, lamps lit now, treasure moved now.

title: The Narrow Door
subtitle: Luke 13:1–35
description: Disasters are refused as verdicts, a bent woman is loosed on the Sabbath, and the journeying Jesus laments over Jerusalem like a hen over chicks.
paragraphs: The news that opens the chapter is an atrocity: Galileans murdered by Pilate at their sacrifices, their blood mixed with the offerings. The tellers expect a verdict on the victims, and Jesus refuses the whole arithmetic of disaster: “Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered this way? No, I tell you. But unless you repent, you too will all perish.” He adds a second disaster of his own, the eighteen crushed when the tower of Siloam fell, and gives it the same interpretation: not worse sinners, and the same warning, “unless you repent, you too will all perish.” Tragedy in Luke is not a ranking of the dead. It is a summons to the living.

The fig tree parable turns the summons into a reprieve with a deadline. A man searches his vineyard fig tree for fruit three years running and finds none, and his order is reasonable: “Therefore cut it down! Why should it use up the soil?” The keeper of the vineyard intercedes with a gardener's patience: “Sir,” the man replied, “leave it alone again this year, until I dig around it and fertilize it. If it bears fruit next year, fine. But if not, you can cut it down.” One more year, with digging and manure, mercy doing work. The parable is left open on purpose: no fourth year is narrated. The hearer is standing in it.

On a Sabbath in a synagogue Jesus calls forward a woman disabled by a spirit for eighteen years, bent over double, unable to stand straight, and before any request from her he declares, “Woman, you are set free from your disability,” and lays his hands on her, and she straightens and glorifies God. The synagogue leader addresses his indignation to the crowd, not to Jesus: “There are six days for work,” he told the crowd. “So come and be healed on those days and not on the Sabbath.” The Lord's reply names the woman what the leader would not: “You hypocrites!” the Lord replied. “Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or donkey from the stall and lead it to water? Then should not this daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has kept bound for eighteen long years, be released from her bondage on the Sabbath day?” A daughter of Abraham, bound by Satan, loosed on the day of rest: every noun in the sentence is an argument. His adversaries are humiliated and the whole crowd rejoices at the glorious things being done.

Two small parables of the kingdom follow, both of hidden growth: the mustard seed a man tossed in his garden that “grew and became a tree, and the birds of the air nested in its branches,” and the leaven a woman mixed into three measures of flour “until all of it was leavened.” Then, traveling through towns toward Jerusalem, he is asked the numbers question, whether only a few will be saved, and answers with effort instead of statistics: “Make every effort to enter through the narrow door. For many, I tell you, will try to enter and will not be able.” The shut door scene that follows is for people who knew him by proximity: we ate and drank with you, you taught in our streets. The master's answer knows no proximity: “I do not know where you are from. Depart from me, all you evildoers.” And the feast they are shut out of fills with the unlikely: “People will come from east and west and north and south, and will recline at the table in the kingdom of God,” and some who are last will be first.

Pharisees bring a warning that Herod wants to kill him, and his reply treats the tetrarch as scenery: “Go tell that fox” that the work continues on schedule, today, tomorrow, and the third day reaching its goal, for a prophet cannot perish outside Jerusalem. Then the journeying pauses for the lament that opens his heart over the destination itself: “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her, how often I have longed to gather your children together as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were unwilling!” Her house is left desolate, and she will not see him again until she says the words of the coming entry: “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord.”

title: The Great Banquet
subtitle: Luke 14:1–35
description: Seats at a Pharisee's table are rearranged by a parable, invited guests excuse themselves out of a feast, and the cost of discipleship is counted.
paragraphs: Another Sabbath, another Pharisee's table, another watchful room, and a man with dropsy standing right in front of Jesus. This time Jesus puts the question to the experts first: “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath or not?” They remain silent. He takes hold of the man, heals him, and sends him on his way, and then asks the question that has ended every one of these scenes: “Which of you whose son or ox falls into a pit on the Sabbath day will not immediately pull him out?” And they were unable to answer. The silence of the lawyers is becoming a refrain in this Gospel, and so is the healing they cannot answer.

Watching the guests choose the places of honor, Jesus tells the seating parable. Do not take the best seat, in case a more distinguished guest has been invited and the host moves you down in humiliation. Instead, “go and sit in the last place, so that your host will come and tell you, ‘Friend, move up to a better place.’” The principle is stated as law: “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the one who humbles himself will be exalted.” Then he turns from the guests to the host, and the instruction applies the same math to the invitation list: when you give a banquet, “do not invite your friends or brothers or relatives or rich neighbors,” who will repay you with invitations of their own. “But when you host a banquet, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind, and you will be blessed. Since they cannot repay you, you will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous.” A guest, charmed, exclaims the obvious beatitude: “Blessed is everyone who will eat at the feast in the kingdom of God.” Jesus answers the exclamation with the parable that gives this episode its name, and it is not a comfortable one.

A man prepares a great banquet and invites many, and at the hour sends his servant with the final word: “Come, for everything is now ready.” Then, one after another, they all begin to make excuses, the politeness indistinguishable from refusal. “I have bought a field, and I need to go see it. Please excuse me.” Five yoke of oxen must be tried out; a man has married a wife and cannot come. Property, business, family, three respectable reasons, three empty seats. The master, angry, changes the guest list on the spot: “Go out quickly into the streets and alleys of the city, and bring in the poor, the crippled, the blind, and the lame,” the exact list Jesus gave the host in the same chapter. The servant reports it done and still room; the order widens past the city: “Go out to the highways and hedges and compel them to come in, so that my house will be full.” And the sentence on the original guests stands: “not one of those men who were invited will taste my banquet.” The feast is filled. It is simply filled with other people.

The chapter closes against the large crowds now traveling with him, with the hardest terms in the Gospel. Twice the sentence ends, he cannot be My disciple: once for the man who comes to Jesus and “does not hate his father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters,” yes, “even his own life,” hate measured against the allegiance being claimed, not against the fourth commandment; and once for the man who does not give up everything he has. Between the two endings stand two calculators: the tower builder, who must “first sit down and count the cost to see if he has the resources to complete it,” lest the unfinished foundation draw ridicule; and the king with ten thousand facing twenty thousand, who sends a delegation while the enemy is still far off. Even salt is given its failure mode: “Salt is good, but if the salt loses its savor, with what will it be seasoned?” It is thrown out. “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.” The banquet is free and the house will be full; following the host out of the banquet is the most expensive decision in the world. Luke sets the two truths side by side and moves on toward the lost sheep.

title: Lost and Found
subtitle: Luke 15:1–32
description: A sheep, a coin, and a son: three lost things, three searches, and a father pleading with the son who stayed home.
paragraphs: The chapter exists because of a complaint. Tax collectors and sinners are gathering around to listen to Jesus, and the Pharisees and scribes grumble the indictment that hangs over the whole Gospel: “This man welcomes sinners and eats with them.” Jesus answers the grumble with three stories about lost things, and the first two are about the seeker's joy. “What man among you, if he has a hundred sheep and loses one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the pasture and go after the one that is lost, until he finds it?” He finds it, puts it joyfully on his shoulders, comes home, and calls his friends and neighbors together: “Rejoice with me, for I have found my lost sheep!” Then heaven's arithmetic: “there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous ones who do not need to repent.” The ninety-nine are not the heroes of the sentence. The one is.

The coin shrinks the flock to a house. A woman with ten silver coins loses one, and she lights a lamp, sweeps the house, and searches carefully until she finds it, and her call to the neighbors is the shepherd's call word for word: “Rejoice with me, for I have found my lost coin.” “In the same way, I tell you, there is joy in the presence of God’s angels over one sinner who repents.” A sheep wanders; a coin is merely lost in the dark of its own house; both are searched for until found, and neither finding is private. Heaven's joy and the woman's party are the same event viewed from two sides.

The third story is the longest parable Jesus tells, and it begins with an outrage disguised as a request. “Father, give me my share of the estate,” the younger son says, asking in effect for his inheritance while his father still lives, and the father divides the property between them without recorded argument. In a distant country the boy squanders everything in wild living, and when famine strips the country he hires himself out to feed pigs, the bottom of the world for a Jewish son, and envies the pigs their pods: “He longed to fill his belly with the pods the pigs were eating, but no one would give him a thing.” Then the turning, described as sanity returning: “How many of my father’s hired servants have plenty of food, but here I am, starving to death!” He rehearses a speech, sin confessed against heaven and against his father, sonship renounced, a hired servant's place requested, and he gets up and goes home with the speech ready.

The speech never gets finished, because the father was watching the road. “But while he was still in the distance, his father saw him and was filled with compassion. He ran to his son, embraced him, and kissed him.” The son begins, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son,” and there the rehearsed words stop, swallowed by the father's orders to the servants: “Quick! Bring the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his finger and sandals on his feet. Bring the fattened calf and kill it. Let us feast and celebrate. For this son of mine was dead and is alive again! He was lost and is found!” Robe, ring, sandals, calf: sonship restored at a run, before the apology could negotiate terms. The hired-servant clause is never spoken again.

Outside the house stands the older son, home from the field, hearing music and dancing, and refusing to go in when he learns the reason. The father comes out to him too, and pleads, and receives the ledger of the dutiful: “Look, all these years I have served you and never disobeyed a commandment of yours. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours returns from squandering your wealth with prostitutes, you kill the fattened calf for him!” The father answers the ledger with presence: “Son, you are always with me,” the father said, “and all that is mine is yours.” And then the reason that governs the feast: “it was fitting to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.” Luke ends the parable there, mid-conversation, the older son's decision unrecorded, because the men it was told to are standing in his place, outside a celebration, deciding. The grumble of the chapter's first verse has been answered by a father pleading on a doorstep. Whether the grumblers come in is the verse Luke does not write.

title: The Rich Man and Lazarus
subtitle: Luke 16:1–31
description: A shrewd manager spends his last authority well, money's limits are stated, and a beggar at a gate is named where a rich man is not.
paragraphs: The chapter opens on a manager about to be fired for wasting his master's possessions, called in to render his account: “What is this I hear about you? Turn in an account of your management, for you cannot be manager any longer.” The man thinks fast and honestly about his own limits: “I am too weak to dig and too ashamed to beg.” His solution is to spend his remaining authority on other people's debts, calling in his master's debtors one by one and cutting their bills while he still holds the pen: “Take your bill,” said the manager, “sit down quickly, and write fifty,” a hundred measures of oil halved; a hundred of wheat written down to eighty. When he is out, the debtors will owe him their welcome. The shock of the parable is the master's response: “The master commended the dishonest manager because he had acted shrewdly.” Jesus' application turns the shrewdness heavenward: “use worldly wealth to make friends for yourselves so that when it is gone, they will welcome you into eternal dwellings.” Money is a wasting asset with one durable use: people. Faithfulness scales from little to much, and the chapter ends the section with the impossibility stated flat: “No servant can serve two masters.” And at the saying's end, “You cannot serve both God and money.”

The Pharisees, “who were lovers of money,” scoff at all of this, and the scoffing draws the diagnosis: “You are the ones who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts. For what is prized among men is detestable before God.” The Law, he insists, has not been retired by the kingdom's arrival: “it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for a single stroke of a pen to drop out of the Law,” and the divorce saying attached to the paragraph stands as one unbending example of its continuing edge.

Then the second Lazarus in Luke, and the only man named in any parable. “Now there was a rich man dressed in purple and fine linen, who lived each day in joyous splendor. And a beggar named Lazarus lay at his gate, covered with sores and longing to be fed with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table. Even the dogs came and licked his sores.” No conversation is recorded between them, no cruelty, no kindness, only proximity: a gate, a table, a man regularly carried past another man's dinner. “One day the beggar died and was carried by the angels to Abraham’s side. And the rich man also died and was buried.” The reversal is total and immediate. In Hades, in torment, the rich man looks up and sees Abraham far away with Lazarus at his side, and the first words of the only prayer in the parable are addressed not to God but across the divide: “Father Abraham, have mercy on me and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue. For I am in agony in this fire.” Even in torment he is giving Lazarus errands. He knows the beggar's name. He had always known it.

Abraham's answer is memory and geometry: “Child, remember that during your lifetime you received your good things, while Lazarus received bad things. But now he is comforted here, while you are in agony.” And the divide cannot be crossed in either direction, for “a great chasm has been fixed between us and you, so that even those who wish cannot cross from here to you, nor can anyone cross from there to us.” The rich man thinks of his five brothers, still alive, still at tables, and begs for Lazarus to be sent to warn them, and Abraham's refusal is the parable's true point: “They have Moses and the Prophets; let your brothers listen to them.” The dead man is certain a resurrection would do what Scripture has not: “No, father Abraham,” he said, “but if someone is sent to them from the dead, they will repent.” The last line of the parable is Abraham's, and it hangs over everything that follows in this Gospel, over an empty tomb most of all: “If they do not listen to Moses and the Prophets, they will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead.”

title: Where Are the Other Nine?
subtitle: Luke 17:1–18:14
description: Forgiveness seven times a day, ten lepers cleansed and one foreigner back, the kingdom in their midst, and two men praying in the temple.
paragraphs: The teaching that opens the chapter is about the damage one disciple can do to another. “It is inevitable that stumbling blocks will come, but woe to the one through whom they come!” The millstone warning follows, better drowned than to trip one of the little ones, and then the obligation turns inward on the victim: “If your brother sins, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him. Even if he sins against you seven times in a day, and seven times returns to say, ‘I repent,’ you must forgive him.” Seven offences, seven returns, seven forgiven, all before nightfall. The apostles' response is the most honest prayer in the chapter: “Increase our faith!” And the Lord's answer relocates the problem from quantity to kind: “If you have faith the size of a mustard seed, you can say to this mulberry tree, ‘Be uprooted and planted in the sea,’ and it will obey you.” Forgiving like that does not need more faith. It needs real faith, seed-sized and alive.

The servant parable that follows strips the reward out of duty. A servant comes in from plowing; no master seats him at the table first or thanks him for the day's work; he serves the meal, then eats. “So you also, when you have done everything commanded of you, should say, ‘We are unworthy servants; we have only done our duty.’” It is the temper of the whole journey: obedience is not a currency, and neither, as the next scene will show, is gratitude a given.

On the road again, passing between Samaria and Galilee, ten lepers meet him at a village edge, standing at the distance their disease required, and their cry is the prayer of this Gospel: “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!” His answer is an instruction, not a touch: “Go, show yourselves to the priests.” And as they went, they were cleansed, all ten, healing arriving mid-obedience. One of them, seeing he was healed, turned back praising God in a loud voice and fell facedown at Jesus' feet in thanksgiving, “and he was a Samaritan.” The questions Jesus asks are the episode's title and its sting: “Were not all ten cleansed?” Jesus asked. “Where then are the other nine? Was no one found except this foreigner to return and give glory to God?” Nine men are walking to the priests with exactly what they asked for. The foreigner has something more, and Jesus names it as he sends him on: “Rise and go; your faith has made you well!” All ten were cleansed. One came back, and only one hears that word, well.

Asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come, Jesus refuses the timetable: “The kingdom of God will not come with observable signs. Nor will people say, ‘Look, here it is,’ or ‘There it is.’ For you see, the kingdom of God is in your midst.” Then, to the disciples alone, he speaks of days when they will long to see one of the days of the Son of Man and not see it, and of false alarms not to chase, because the true coming needs no pointer: “For just as the lightning flashes and lights up the sky from one end to the other, so will be the Son of Man in His day. But first He must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation.” The days of Noah and of Lot are his pictures of the ordinary world on the edge of judgment: eating and drinking, marrying, buying and selling, planting and building, up to the very day. “Remember Lot’s wife!” Flight that looks back is not flight. “Whoever tries to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life will preserve it.” Two in one bed, two grinding at the mill, one taken and the other left, and to the disciples' question, “Where, Lord?” the answer is a proverb of carrion: “Wherever there is a carcass, there the vultures will gather.” Judgment will be as findable as that.

Luke closes the stretch with two parables on prayer, told, Luke says, for their “need to pray at all times and not lose heart.” The unjust judge, who neither fears God nor respects men, is worn down by a widow's perpetual return: “Give me justice against my adversary,” until he grants it to be rid of her. “Listen to the words of the unjust judge,” the Lord says. “Will not God bring about justice for His elect who cry out to Him day and night?” The parable's last line turns it into a question about the listeners themselves: “Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will He find faith on earth?” The second parable is aimed at those who “trusted in their own righteousness and viewed others with contempt,” and it is set in the temple at prayer. The Pharisee thanks God with a list of the men he is not: “God, I thank You that I am not like other men,” swindlers, evildoers, adulterers, “or even like this tax collector,” and then recites his own record: “I fast twice a week and pay tithes of all that I acquire.” The tax collector stands at a distance, will not lift his eyes, beats his breast, and manages seven words: “God, have mercy on me, a sinner!” “I tell you, this man, rather than the Pharisee, went home justified.” The maxim from the banquet chapter seals it, exaltation humbled and humility exalted, and the road to Jerusalem continues.

title: What Must I Do to Inherit Eternal Life?
subtitle: Luke 18:15–43
description: Children are welcomed, a rich ruler goes away sad, the third prediction is not understood, and a blind beggar sees and follows.
paragraphs: People are bringing even their babies to Jesus for his touch, and the disciples rebuke them for it, gatekeeping again. Jesus overrules the gate: “Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of God belongs to such as these.” And the principle he lays down reverses the journey's ladder entirely: “anyone who does not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will never enter it.” The kingdom is received the way a child receives everything, empty-handed. The next man through the gate brings a résumé.

A certain ruler asks the chapter's great question in its plainest form: “Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?” Jesus stops on the greeting first: “Why do you call Me good?” Jesus replied. “No one is good except God alone.” Then the commandments of the second table, the ones between man and man: “Do not commit adultery, do not murder, do not steal, do not bear false witness, honor your father and mother.” The ruler's answer is confident and, within its limits, true: “All these I have kept from my youth,” he said. Jesus' reply honors the keeping by finding the one thing it has been protecting him from: “You still lack one thing: Sell everything you own and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow Me.” The man becomes very sad, “because he was extremely wealthy,” and he goes nowhere. Luke does not record that he sold anything or followed. The one thing lacked was everything.

Seeing his sadness, Jesus pronounces the difficulty in the Gospel's sharpest image: “How hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom of God! Indeed, it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God.” The bystanders hear the impossibility correctly: “Who then can be saved?” And the answer is the door the camel cannot fit through, opened from the other side: “What is impossible with man is possible with God.” Peter, counting the contrast, says what the Twelve have in fact done: “Look,” said Peter, “we have left all we had to follow You.” The promise given them is proportionate: “no one who has left home or wife or brothers or parents or children for the sake of the kingdom of God will fail to receive many times more in this age” and in the age to come, eternal life. Leaving is not loss, in this Gospel's accounting. It is the ruler's road, taken in the other direction.

Then, taking the Twelve aside yet again, Jesus tells them the destination plainly, the third time on this road: “Look, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything the prophets have written about the Son of Man will be fulfilled. He will be delivered over to the Gentiles and will be mocked and insulted and spit upon. They will flog Him and kill Him, and on the third day He will rise again.” Luke's comment on the clearest prediction yet is total non-comprehension: the disciples did not understand any of these things, the meaning was hidden from them. The man who is about to see cannot yet be seen by the men closest to him, and the contrast is the next scene.

Near Jericho a blind beggar sits by the road, unnamed in Luke's telling, and hearing the crowd he asks what is happening. “Jesus of Nazareth is passing by,” they told him. His cry uses the title the crowd did not give him: “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” Those in front rebuke him to silence, the disciples' gesture repeated by strangers, and he cries all the louder, “Son of David, have mercy on me!” Jesus stops, has him brought, and asks the question he asks everyone who will answer it honestly: “What do you want Me to do for you?” “Lord,” he said, “let me see again.” “Receive your sight!” Jesus replied. “Your faith has healed you.” Immediately he received his sight and followed Jesus, glorifying God, and all the people gave praise to God. A rich ruler went away sad with his eyes open; a blind beggar follows down the road, seeing. Jericho is one town away from the little man in the tree.

title: To Seek and to Save the Lost
subtitle: Luke 19:1–27
description: A chief tax collector comes down from a tree a changed man, and a nobleman's minas test his servants while the kingdom delays.
paragraphs: Jericho's chief tax collector is rich, hated, and too short to see over a crowd. Zacchaeus runs on ahead of the procession, a grown man of standing climbing a sycamore tree like a boy, just to see who Jesus is. When Jesus reaches the place, he looks up and does the calling himself: “Zacchaeus, hurry down, for I must stay at your house today.” Zacchaeus hurries down and welcomes him joyfully, and the crowd grumbles the familiar grumble, now at its sharpest address: “He has gone to be the guest of a sinful man!” No invitation had been negotiated, no repentance auditioned. The seeker had been sought.

Inside the house, the fruit appears without being demanded. Zacchaeus stands and makes his declaration to the Lord, present tense, a policy, not a promise: “Look, Lord, half of my possessions I give to the poor, and if I have cheated anyone, I will repay it fourfold.” Half his estate to the poor and fourfold restitution to the cheated, from the chief tax collector of Jericho, on the day Jesus came to lunch. Jesus' verdict on the house is the journey's mission statement arriving at a saved address: “Today salvation has come to this house, because this man too is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.” Too is the loaded word. The grumblers had written him out of Abraham's family; Jesus writes him back in, and the lost sheep of chapter 15 turns out to have been up a tree in Jericho.

Because they are near Jerusalem and the crowd thinks the kingdom of God will appear immediately, Jesus tells one more parable, and it is about delay and accounting. A nobleman goes to a distant country to receive a kingship; before leaving he gives ten servants a mina each, a small sum, with instructions: “Conduct business with this until I return,” he said. His subjects, meanwhile, send a delegation after him: “We do not want this man to rule over us.” On his return as king, the servants render their accounts. The first mina has made ten: “Well done, good servant! Because you have been faithful in a very small matter, you shall have authority over ten cities.” The second has made five, and receives five cities. The proportion is the teaching: faithfulness in a very small matter, rewarded in a currency of cities.

The third servant produces the mina itself, kept laid away in a piece of cloth, and his defense is a character reference for his master: “Master, here is your mina, which I have laid away in a piece of cloth. For I was afraid of you, because you are a harsh man. You withdraw what you did not deposit and reap what you did not sow.” The master judges him out of his own theology: “You wicked servant, I will judge you by your own words.” If you believed I was that kind of master, the bank was the least you could do, and the interest would have been waiting. The mina is taken and given to the servant with ten, over the bystanders' protest that he already has ten, and the principle stands where the rich ruler's story left it: “everyone who has will be given more; but the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him.” Then the parable ends where parables rarely end, with the delegation's answer. The enemies who would not have him rule over them are brought and slain before him. Luke lets the king's sentence stand in the story unsoftened, the road turns up out of Jericho toward the city that is about to render the same refusal, and the kingdom does not appear immediately after all.

title: He Wept Over the City
subtitle: Luke 19:28–48
description: A borrowed colt, a shouting multitude, tears over Jerusalem, and a temple cleared to be a house of prayer again.
paragraphs: The ascent from Jericho ends with a borrowed colt. At Bethphage and Bethany, on the Mount of Olives, Jesus sends two disciples ahead with precise instructions: “Go into the village ahead of you, and as you enter it, you will find a colt tied there, on which no one has ever sat. Untie it and bring it here.” And for the owners' inevitable question he gives them a password that is also a claim: “The Lord needs it.” They find it just as he told them, and untying it they are asked, and they answer with the words given, and that is the whole negotiation. The disciples throw their cloaks over the colt and set Jesus on it, and as he rides, people spread their cloaks on the road before him, a carpet of garments down the western slope.

At the descent, the whole multitude of the disciples begins to praise God joyfully in a loud voice for all the miracles they had seen, and Luke's version of the shout names the rider outright: “Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord!” “Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!” Some Pharisees in the crowd ask him to rebuke his disciples, and the answer removes the option: “I tell you,” He answered, “if they remain silent, the very stones will cry out.” The acclamation is not enthusiasm that can be managed. It is geology waiting its turn.

Then the King sees the city and weeps over it, the second time tears are recorded of him, and the words through the weeping are an unfulfilled wish and a sentence: “If only you had known on this day what would bring you peace! But now it is hidden from your eyes.” What follows is a siege described in advance, in an engineer's terms: “For the days will come upon you when your enemies will barricade you and surround you and hem you in on every side. They will level you to the ground,” you and the children within your walls, “They will not leave one stone on another, because you did not recognize the time of your visitation from God.” Visitation is Luke's word for what this day was: God come to his city in the person of its king, unrecognized at the moment of arrival, while the stones were still being kept silent by the shouting.

He enters the temple courts and begins driving out those who were selling there, and Luke gives the act its two proof texts in one breath: “It is written: ‘My house will be a house of prayer.’ But you have made it ‘a den of robbers.’” Prayer house or robbers' den: the cleansing is a verdict on which of the two the courts had become. Afterward he teaches in the temple every day, an occupation the authorities can see and cannot stop, for the chief priests, scribes, and leaders of the people are intent on killing him, yet “they could not find a way to do so, because all the people hung on His words.” The weeping is over. The teaching days in the temple have begun, and every day of them is numbered.

title: He Is Not the God of the Dead
subtitle: Luke 20:1–47
description: Authority challenged and returned, tenants who kill the son, Caesar's coin, and the resurrection proved from the burning bush.
paragraphs: The temple days open with a direct challenge. As Jesus teaches the people and proclaims the gospel, the chief priests, scribes, and elders confront him: “Tell us,” they said, “by what authority are You doing these things, and who gave You this authority?” He answers with a counter-question that puts the confrontation back in their court: John's baptism, “was it from heaven, or from men?” Their deliberation is recorded with unusual candor. From heaven invites the rebuke, “Why did you not believe him?” From men invites the stones of a people convinced John was a prophet. So the Sanhedrin's scholars answer the question of authority with an admission: they did not know. “Neither will I tell you by what authority I am doing these things,” Jesus replied. The men who could not answer about John are told they cannot be answered about him.

Then to the people he tells the parable of the vineyard, the Gospel's own history in disguise. A man plants a vineyard, rents it to tenants, and goes away for a long time; at harvest he sends a servant for his share of the fruit, and the tenants beat him and send him away empty. A second is beaten and shamed, a third wounded and thrown out. The owner's deliberation is the story's heart: “What shall I do?” asked the owner of the vineyard. “I will send my beloved son. Perhaps they will respect him.” The tenants read the son's arrival as opportunity: “This is the heir. Let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.” They throw him out of the vineyard and kill him, and Jesus asks the crowd itself for the verdict: “What then will the owner of the vineyard do to them? He will come and kill those tenants and give the vineyard to others.” The people recoil: “May such a thing never happen!” And the answer is Scripture's own picture of rejection reversed: “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.” And the warning attached to it: “Everyone who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces, but he on whom it falls will be crushed.” The scribes and chief priests know the parable was spoken against them, and want him arrested that very hour, and are afraid of the people. So the parable works exactly as told: the tenants restrain themselves only by calculation.

The spies come next, pretending sincerity, hoping to catch a word for the governor. Their question is a fork with Rome on one tine and the crowd on the other: “Is it lawful for us to pay taxes to Caesar or not?” He sees through the duplicity and asks for the coin itself: “Show Me a denarius. Whose image and inscription are on it?” “Caesar’s,” they answered. “Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.” The trap closes on air, and the spies, amazed at his answer, fall silent. Their silence is the sound of the fork breaking.

Then the Sadducees, who say there is no resurrection, bring their riddle: seven brothers in turn marrying one widow under the law of Moses, all dying childless, and in the resurrection whose wife will she be. Jesus dismantles the premise rather than the arithmetic: “The sons of this age marry and are given in marriage. But those who are considered worthy to share in the age to come and in the resurrection from the dead will neither marry nor be given in marriage. In fact, they can no longer die, because they are like the angels.” Then he proves the resurrection out of their own accepted Scripture, meeting Moses with Moses: at the burning bush, the Lord is called “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,” centuries after all three were buried. “He is not the God of the dead, but of the living, for to Him all are alive.” Some of the scribes, opponents an hour ago, answer honestly: “Teacher, You have spoken well!” And no one dares question him further.

Jesus takes the last question himself, and it is about David's son. “How can it be said that the Christ is the Son of David? For David himself says in the book of Psalms: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet.”’ Thus David calls Him ‘Lord.’ So how can He be David’s son?” No answer is recorded, from anyone. Then, in the hearing of all the people, he warns his disciples about the class that has spent the chapter questioning him: “Beware of the scribes,” the long robes, the greetings, the chief seats, and underneath the pageantry the crime that seals the warning: “They defraud widows of their houses, and for a show make lengthy prayers. These men will receive greater condemnation.” A widow appears next in Luke, and she is at the treasury with two small coins.

title: Heaven and Earth Will Pass Away
subtitle: Luke 21:1–38
description: A widow's two coins outweigh a treasury, the temple's stones are doomed, and the disciples are told to stand up and lift their heads.
paragraphs: The chapter opens at the treasury, where Jesus is watching people give. The rich put in their gifts, and he sees a poor widow put in two small copper coins, and his commentary revalues the whole treasury: “Truly I tell you,” He said, “this poor widow has put in more than all the others. For they all contributed out of their surplus, but she out of her poverty has put in all she had to live on.” More than all the others, measured not by amount but by remainder: everyone else kept a surplus; she kept nothing. It is the last person Jesus commends in the temple, and she is the widow the scribes defraud, giving everything she has to live on to the house of God.

Some of the disciples are admiring the temple itself, the beautiful stones and consecrated gifts, and the admiration draws the sentence the weeping had already pronounced: “As for what you see here, the time will come when not one stone will be left on another; every one will be thrown down.” The question follows naturally, on the Mount of Olives: “Teacher,” they asked, “when will these things happen? And what will be the sign that they are about to take place?” His answer begins with a warning against the answers: “See to it that you are not deceived. For many will come in My name, claiming, ‘I am He,’ and, ‘The time is near.’ Do not follow them.” Wars and rebellions will be read as the end, wrongly: “These things must happen first, but the end is not imminent.” Then the catalog widens, nation against nation, earthquakes, famines, pestilences, fearful sights and great signs from heaven, and before any of it, the disciples' own portion: “But before all this, they will seize you and persecute you. On account of My name they will deliver you to the synagogues and prisons, and they will bring you before kings and governors. This will be your opportunity to serve as witnesses.” Persecution is reframed as a pulpit. The defense is not to be rehearsed: “So make up your mind not to worry beforehand how to defend yourselves. For I will give you speech and wisdom that none of your adversaries will be able to resist or contradict.” Betrayal will come from inside the family, and some will be put to death, and the paradox holds both facts at once: “Yet not even a hair of your head will perish. By your patient endurance you will gain your souls.”

Jerusalem's own sign is military and unmistakable: “But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, you will know that her desolation is near.” Then flight, urgently, Judea to the mountains, the city emptied, the country kept out, because “these are the days of vengeance, to fulfill all that is written.” The exiles will fall by the sword and be led captive into all the nations, “And Jerusalem will be trodden down by the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled.” The until is load-bearing: the trampling has a term. Beyond it stand the cosmic signs, sun and moon and stars, the sea roaring, men fainting from fear, the powers of the heavens shaken, “At that time they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory.” And for the disciples watching it begin, the instruction is posture: “When these things begin to happen, stand up and lift up your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.”

The fig tree is the discourse's own reading lesson: leaves mean summer, and these things mean nearness. “So also, when you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near.” The solemn guarantee follows, “this generation will not pass away until all these things have happened,” and then the sentence this episode takes its title from, the temple's stones and the whole creation weighed against his sentences: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will never pass away.” The closing watch returns to chapter 12's lamps: “But watch yourselves, or your hearts will be weighed down by dissipation, drunkenness, and the worries of life,” for the day will spring like a snare on all who dwell on the earth. “So keep watch at all times, and pray that you may have the strength to escape all that is about to happen and to stand before the Son of Man.” The frame Luke gives the discourse is a rhythm: every day Jesus taught at the temple, every evening he went out to the Mount of Olives, and early each morning all the people came to hear him. Within days, the pattern will break at night on that mountain.

title: I Have Earnestly Desired
subtitle: Luke 22:1–38
description: Judas agrees on a price, the Passover is prepared, the body and the cup are given, and Peter is promised a turning back before he falls.
paragraphs: The feast of Unleavened Bread is approaching, and the chief priests and scribes are looking for a way to put Jesus to death, blocked as always by their fear of the people. Luke names the opening that unblocks them without softening it: “Then Satan entered Judas Iscariot, who was one of the Twelve.” Judas goes to the chief priests and temple officers to discuss how he might betray Jesus to them; they are delighted and agree to give him money; and Judas consents and begins watching for an opportunity in the absence of a crowd. The price is agreed in one verse, without a number. Luke keeps the number for Matthew's telling. Here the bargain is the fact, and the feast goes forward over it.

On the day the Passover lamb was to be sacrificed, Jesus sends Peter and John with instructions in his now familiar pattern: “Go and make preparations for us to eat the Passover.” A man carrying a jug of water will meet them in the city; follow him; say to the owner of the house, “The Teacher asks: Where is the guest room, where I may eat the Passover with My disciples?” He will show them a large upper room, already furnished. They go and find it just as he told them, as always, and prepare the Passover there, while somewhere else in the city another preparation, agreed for money, is also complete.

At the table, the desire is stated before the suffering: “I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you before My suffering. For I tell you that I will not eat it again until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God.” He takes a cup, gives thanks, and has them divide it among themselves, with the vow: “I will not drink of the fruit of the vine from now on until the kingdom of God comes.” Then the bread, broken and given with the words that have carried the meal ever since: “This is My body, given for you; do this in remembrance of Me.” And after supper the cup again: “This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is poured out for you.” Only then, with the covenant spoken over the table, comes the shadow across it: “Look! The hand of My betrayer is with Mine on the table. Indeed, the Son of Man will go as it has been determined, but woe to that man who betrays Him.” Determined, and woe: Luke sets sovereignty and responsibility side by side in one verse and resolves neither. The apostles' response is to question among themselves which of them could do it.

The questioning slides, incredibly, into a dispute about which of them should be considered the greatest, at the table where the body and blood have just been given. His answer redefines the scale: the kings of the Gentiles lord it over their subjects and call themselves benefactors; “But you shall not be like them. Instead, the greatest among you should be like the youngest, and the one who leads like the one who serves. For who is greater, the one who reclines at the table or the one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines? But I am among you as one who serves.” Then, to these same disputing men, the promise: “You are the ones who have stood by Me in My trials. And I bestow on you a kingdom, just as My Father has bestowed one on Me, so that you may eat and drink at My table in My kingdom and sit on thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” Servants at his table here; kings at his table there; the order matters and is not reversed.

The sifting is announced to Simon by name, twice: “Simon, Simon, Satan has asked to sift all of you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, Simon, that your faith will not fail. And when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers.” Peter's reply is total confidence: “Lord,” said Peter, “I am ready to go with You even to prison and to death.” The prediction answers the confidence precisely: “I tell you, Peter, the rooster will not crow today until you have denied three times that you know Me.” The turned back is already promised inside the failure, prayed for in advance. Then the equipment changes: the men sent out empty-handed on the roads, who lacked nothing, are now to take purse and bag and, lacking one, sell a cloak to buy a sword, because Scripture is reaching its fulfillment: “And He was numbered with the transgressors.” Two swords are produced from somewhere among them. “That is enough,” He answered. The table empties into the night, toward the mountain where the prayer is waiting.

title: Rise and Pray
subtitle: Luke 22:39–71
description: Sweat like drops of blood, an ear healed in the arresting crowd, three denials by a courtyard fire, and a council that convicts on his own words.
paragraphs: As usual, Luke says, Jesus goes out to the Mount of Olives, and the disciples follow him, and his first word at the place is the episode's title: “Pray that you will not enter into temptation.” He withdraws about a stone's throw, kneels, and prays the prayer the whole night hangs on: “Father, if You are willing, take this cup from Me. Yet not My will, but Yours be done.” Luke alone records what the prayer cost and what it drew: an angel from heaven appears to him and strengthens him, and in his anguish he prays more earnestly, “and His sweat became like drops of blood falling to the ground.” The physician's Gospel keeps the detail that reads like a diagnosis. He rises and returns to disciples asleep, exhausted from sorrow, and the command is repeated to men who could not obey it the first time: “Why are you sleeping?” He asked. “Get up and pray so that you will not enter into temptation.”

While he is still speaking, the crowd arrives, led by Judas, one of the Twelve, who approaches to kiss him. “Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?” The men around Jesus read the moment faster than they had read anything all night: “Lord, should we strike with our swords?” And one of them, before any answer, strikes the servant of the high priest and cuts off his right ear. Jesus' response is the last healing of his ministry and it is performed on an enemy in the act of arresting him: “No more of this!” And he touched the man's ear and healed him. Then to the chief priests, temple officers, and elders, the protest that defines the arrest's timing: “Have you come out with swords and clubs as you would against an outlaw? Every day I was with you in the temple courts, and you did not lay a hand on Me. But this hour belongs to you and to the power of darkness.” The hour is theirs. The darkness is named as a power. He is seized, led away, taken to the house of the high priest, and Peter follows at a distance.

The courtyard fire is where the sifting happens. Seated among the household staff in the firelight, Peter is identified three times in about an hour, each time by someone with no authority at all. A servant girl, looking intently: “This man also was with Him,” she said. “Woman, I do not know Him,” he said. Someone else: “You also are one of them.” “Man, I am not.” A third, insisting, with the accent as evidence: “Certainly this man was with Him, for he too is a Galilean.” “Man, I do not know what you are talking about,” Peter replied. “And immediately, while he was still speaking, the rooster crowed. And the Lord turned and looked at Peter.” Luke's look crosses the courtyard without a word, and Peter remembers the sentence spoken at the table: “Before the rooster crows today, you will deny Me three times.” He went outside and wept bitterly. The prayer at the table had already named this moment and what lay past it: when you have turned back. The weeping is the turning beginning.

Inside, the men holding Jesus mock and beat him, blindfold him, and play their game with a prophet's gift: “Prophesy! Who hit You?” And they say many other blasphemous things against him through what is left of the night. At daybreak the council of the elders, chief priests and scribes together, leads him into their Sanhedrin: “If You are the Christ, tell us.” His answer predicts their unbelief and refuses their procedure: “If I tell you, you will not believe. And if I ask you a question, you will not answer. But from now on the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God.” They all ask the one question left: “Are You then the Son of God?” He replied, “You say that I am.” And the council concludes the trial in one sentence: “Why do we need any more testimony?” they declared. “We have heard it for ourselves from His own lips.” The charge is set. What remains is finding a court that can kill, and a governor who can be made to care.

title: They Became Friends That Day
subtitle: Luke 23:1–25
description: Herod gets no word at all, Pilate finds no guilt three times, and the crowd's clamor prevails over both courts.
paragraphs: The whole council rises and leads Jesus to Pilate, and the charges they bring have been translated for a Roman ear: “We found this man subverting our nation, forbidding payment of taxes to Caesar, and proclaiming Himself to be Christ, a King.” The middle charge is the tell. Luke's readers sat in the temple court when Jesus said, give to Caesar what is Caesar's, and watched the spies fall silent; the council now accuses him of the opposite. Politics is the only language the governor can be made to hear, so treason is what they speak. Pilate asks the defendant one question: “Are You the King of the Jews?” “You have said so,” Jesus replied. And the governor's first verdict is immediate: “I find no basis for a charge against this man.” The accusers insist, widening the map, he stirs up the people all over Judea, beginning in Galilee and coming all the way here, and the word Galilee gives Pilate an exit he is glad to take.

Learning that Jesus is under Herod's jurisdiction, Pilate sends him to Herod, who happens to be in Jerusalem. Herod is greatly pleased. He has wanted to see Jesus for a long time and “was hoping to see Him perform a miracle,” one sign, Herod the fox receiving at last the performer his household had executed John to silence. Herod questions him at great length, and Jesus, who answered Pilate, gives Herod nothing at all; not one word is recorded. The chief priests and scribes stand there vehemently accusing him into the silence, and Herod and his soldiers fill it with ridicule, dressing him in a fine robe as a joke king and sending him back. Luke closes the audience with the episode's title, the strangest fruit of the trial: “That day Herod and Pilate became friends; before this time they had been enemies.” Two rulers who could agree on nothing else made their peace over the man both of them found innocent.

Pilate reassembles the chief priests, rulers, and people and states the double verdict formally: “You brought me this man as one who was inciting the people to rebellion. I have examined Him here in your presence and found Him not guilty of your charges against Him. Neither has Herod, for he sent Him back to us. As you can see, He has done nothing deserving of death. Therefore I will punish Him and release Him.” The crowd answers in unison: “Away with this man! Release Barabbas to us!” Barabbas, Luke notes in a parenthesis, had been imprisoned for insurrection in the city, and for murder: the actual crimes of the charge sheet, attached to the man the crowd requests. Pilate, wanting to release Jesus, addresses them again, and they keep shouting, “Crucify Him! Crucify Him!” A third time he reasons with them: “What evil has this man done? I have found in Him no offense worthy of death. So after I punish Him, I will release Him.” But they were insistent, demanding with loud voices, and “their clamor prevailed.” So Pilate sentenced that their demand be met. He released the one imprisoned for insurrection and murder, as they requested, “and he handed Jesus over to their will.” Three verdicts of innocence are on the record, from the governor's own mouth, twice confirmed by a second court. The sentence is crucifixion anyway. Luke lets the record stand exactly that crooked.

title: Father, Forgive Them
subtitle: Luke 23:26–56
description: A prayer for the executioners, a criminal promised Paradise today, darkness at noon, and a borrowed tomb before the Sabbath.
paragraphs: On the way out they seize a passerby, Simon of Cyrene, coming in from the country, and lay the cross on him to carry behind Jesus. A great multitude follows, including women mourning and wailing for him, and Jesus turns to them on the road to his own execution with a redirection of their tears: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for Me, but weep for yourselves and for your children.” The days are coming, he tells them, when the barren will be called blessed, when people will beg the mountains to fall on them and the hills to cover them, the siege he wept over the city now spoken to its daughters. And the proverb that explains the green wood: “For if men do these things while the tree is green, what will happen when it is dry?” If this is what the city does to the innocent in a season of green, the dry season's fire is not hard to imagine.

At the place called The Skull they crucify him, with two criminals, one on his right and the other on his left, and the first recorded word from the cross in Luke is a prayer for the men driving the nails: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” Beneath the prayer, his garments are divided by casting lots. The people stand watching, and the rulers sneer the theology of the taunt: “He saved others; let Him save Himself if He is the Christ of God, the Chosen One.” The soldiers join in, offering sour wine, with their version: “If You are the King of the Jews,” they said, “save Yourself!” Above him is posted the inscription, Pilate's answer to the charge sheet, in the form of a title: this is the King of the Jews. Every voice at the cross is demanding the same miracle the devil demanded in the wilderness and Herod demanded in the palace, a saving of himself, and the forgiveness already spoken covers the demanders.

One of the criminals hanging beside him heaps abuse on him with the same request in a dying man's form: “Are You not the Christ?” he said. “Save Yourself and us!” The other criminal rebukes him, and his speech is the most theologically exact confession at the cross: “Do you not even fear God, since you are under the same judgment? We are punished justly, for we are receiving what our actions deserve. But this man has done nothing wrong.” Justice for us, innocence for him, and then the request, in full knowledge of what he is asking a crucified man: “Jesus, remember me when You come into Your kingdom!” The answer exceeds the request in every dimension: “Truly I tell you, today you will be with Me in Paradise.” He asked to be remembered someday, in a kingdom; he is promised company today, in Paradise. The first person taken into the kingdom in this Gospel, carried in over the protest of nobody, is a confessed criminal with hours to live and nothing to offer but the asking.

About the sixth hour, darkness comes over all the land until the ninth, the sun darkened, and the veil of the temple is torn down the middle. Then Jesus calls out in a loud voice his last words in Luke, which are a child's bedtime psalm spoken as a deposit: “Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit.” And having said this, he breathed his last. The centurion, watching, glorifies God with Luke's verdict on the whole proceeding: “Surely this was a righteous man.” Not a king acknowledged, in this Gospel's account, but innocence declared by the executioner. The crowds who had gathered for the spectacle return home beating their breasts, and all those who knew him, including the women who had followed him from Galilee, stand at a distance, watching.

The burial is Joseph's doing, a Council member, good and righteous, who had not consented to their decision or action, from Arimathea, himself waiting for the kingdom of God. He goes to Pilate, asks for the body, takes it down, wraps it in linen, and lays it in a rock-cut tomb where no one had yet been laid. It was Preparation Day, and the Sabbath was beginning. The women from Galilee follow and see the tomb and how his body is placed; then they go home and prepare spices and perfumes, and “they rested on the Sabbath, according to the commandment.” The last act of the chapter is obedience at rest, by women who do not yet know what the morning holds, keeping the Sabbath over a sealed tomb.

title: On the Road to Emmaus
subtitle: Luke 24:1–35
description: Women disbelieved, Peter wondering, and two travelers who recognize the stranger only when he breaks the bread.
paragraphs: On the first day of the week, very early in the morning, the women come to the tomb bringing the spices they had prepared, and find the stone rolled away, and when they enter they do not find the body of the Lord Jesus. While they are puzzling over this, two men in radiant apparel stand beside them, and as the women bow their faces to the ground in terror, the men ask the question the whole Gospel has been building toward: “Why do you look for the living among the dead? He is not here; He has risen!” The evidence offered is not the empty tomb but their own memories: “Remember how He told you while He was still in Galilee: ‘The Son of Man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men, and be crucified, and on the third day rise again.’” Then they remembered his words. Resurrection, in Luke's telling, is recognized first as something Jesus had already said, three times on the road, in plain hearing.

The women, Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James, and the others, return and report all of this to the Eleven and to everyone else. “But their words seemed like nonsense to them, and they did not believe the women.” The first witnesses of the resurrection in this Gospel are disbelieved by the apostles themselves, talked over in the same hour they deliver the news. Peter alone moves: he gets up and runs to the tomb, bends down, sees only the linen cloths, and goes away “wondering to himself what had happened.” Wonder is as far as the evidence takes the man who will later be named as the first of the Eleven to see him. The women remembered; Peter wonders; the rest dismiss. Luke stacks the three responses and moves to the road.

That same day two of them are walking to a village called Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem, talking over everything that has happened, and Jesus himself comes up and walks along with them, “But their eyes were kept from recognizing Him.” He asks what they are discussing so intently, and they stand still, faces sad. One of them, named Cleopas, answers with the day's great irony: “Are You the only visitor to Jerusalem who does not know the things that have happened there in recent days?” The only man in Jerusalem who knows exactly what happened is being pitied for missing the news.

Their account, given to the stranger, is accurate in every fact and wrong in its tense: “This man was a prophet, powerful in speech and action before God and all the people. Our chief priests and rulers delivered Him up to the sentence of death, and they crucified Him. But we were hoping He was the One who would redeem Israel.” Were hoping. The women's report is included, angels and all, and the check of the tomb by their companions, and then the five saddest words of the summary: “But Him they did not see.” Then the stranger rebukes the men he has just walked seven miles beside: “O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and then to enter His glory?” And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he explains to them what was written in all the Scriptures about himself, the longest Bible study in the New Testament, entirely unrecorded in its content, delivered to two disappointed men on a country road.

At the village he acts as if he will go farther, and they plead with him: “Stay with us, for it is nearly evening and the day is almost over.” At their table the guest takes over the host's part: he takes bread, speaks a blessing, breaks it, and gives it to them, the feeding of the five thousand and the upper room in four motions. “Then their eyes were opened and they recognized Jesus,” and he disappears from their sight. Recognition comes in the breaking of the bread, not in the exposition, and their verdict on the walk re-reads it entirely: “Were not our hearts burning within us as He spoke with us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” They rise that very hour and walk the seven miles back in the dark to Jerusalem, and find the Eleven gathered with the news already running ahead of them: “The Lord has indeed risen and has appeared to Simon!” And the two tell what had happened on the road, and how they had recognized him in the breaking of the bread. Midnight was coming on. The day was not finished with any of them.

title: Peace to You
subtitle: Luke 24:36–53
description: Flesh and bones and broiled fish, minds opened to the Scriptures, a blessing interrupted by heaven, and joy back in the temple.
paragraphs: While they are still describing these events, Jesus himself stands among them, and his first words to the assembled apostles are the greeting that gives this Gospel its last episode its name: “Peace be with you.” They are startled and frightened, thinking they have seen a spirit, and the proof he offers is not an argument but his wounds: “Why are you troubled,” Jesus asked, “and why do doubts arise in your hearts? Look at My hands and My feet. It is I Myself. Touch Me and see,” for “a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see I have.” And he shows them his hands and his feet. The body that was laid in the tomb is the body in the room, hands and feet marked, flesh and bones offered to their touch. Luke, who began his Gospel by promising an orderly account, ends it by insisting on the evidence of the senses.

They are still in disbelief, and Luke names the reason with a phrase no other account risks: disbelief “because of their joy and amazement.” Joy itself is slowing their belief down. So he asks them the most ordinary question in the chapter: “Do you have anything here to eat?” They give him a piece of broiled fish, and he takes it and eats it in front of them. A spirit does not have flesh and bones; a spirit also does not eat broiled fish. The resurrection is certified in Luke by a meal, as the birth was certified by a manger and the recognition at Emmaus by broken bread.

Then he gives them the hermeneutic of the whole Gospel, and of the book that will follow it: “These are the words I spoke to you while I was still with you: Everything must be fulfilled that is written about Me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms.” And he opens their minds to understand the Scriptures, the same opening that happened to two men's eyes at a village table, now done for the whole company at once. “This is what is written: The Christ will suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, and in His name repentance and forgiveness of sins will be proclaimed to all nations, beginning in Jerusalem. You are witnesses of these things.” Repentance and forgiveness, the twin announcements of Luke's story from John's first sermon to the tax collector's breast-beating prayer, are now the message to be carried out of Jerusalem to all nations, by witnesses. And the equipment for it is a promise and a waiting: “I am sending the promise of My Father upon you. But remain in the city until you have been clothed with power from on high.” The story does not end at the ascension. It pauses in the city, under orders to wait.

He leads them out as far as Bethany, lifts up his hands, and blesses them, and the blessing is interrupted by the departure: “While He was blessing them, He left them and was carried up into heaven.” No farewell speech follows, because the blessing was the speech, left unfinished in their ears on purpose. And they worship him, this company that a few hours before had called the women's report nonsense, and they return to Jerusalem with great joy, “praising God continually in the temple.” Luke's Gospel opened in that temple, with an old priest burning incense and coming out unable to speak. It closes in the same temple, filled with the voices of the witnesses, blessing God without stopping. The next chapter of the story belongs to another book, and it begins where this one ends: in Jerusalem, waiting.
